14.  Public/ Awareness Outreach Programme
 
14.1 The Committee being concerned about some of the projects of the Department of 
Atomic Energy getting adversely affected/delay ed and a few others stuck up since as far 
back as Xth Five Year Plan due to public discontentment, asked the Department about the 
steps taken and Programme, if any, chalked out to deal effectively with the situation.  The 
Committee was informed that the DAE carri ed out a number of public awareness 
activities at a mission mode in a structured manner and through a multi-pronged 
approach.  A number of public awareness programme pursued by the Department over 
the last 5 years consisted of organizing/ pa rticipating in 100 exhibitions in different 
regions of the country; conducting some 145 seminars/workshops for students/ academy, 
general/ rural public, etc.; making of over 15 video films and multimedia presentations, 
organizing all India essay contest in nucle ar science & technol ogy and several essay 
contests and quiz competitions for high-school and college level students, publishing over 
45 publications and about 12 advertisements/ articles in variou s popular magazines 
mostly in various official la nguages, etc.  The Department also informed that it had 
recently chalked out a public outreach programme that included:- 
• Regular advertisements in TV channels & print media 
• Media workshops 
• Fifteen public outreach centres at DAE facilities ( during the XII plan period ) 
One such centre to be established at the DAE Head Quarters, Mumbai. 
• Displaying positive messages about Atomic Energy on all departmental vehicles 
• Hoardings to be put up in its premises and residential complexes 
• Exploiting the social media (FB, Twitter, mass e-mailing, mass messaging) 
advertisements, etc. 
14.2  While the Committee appreciates the e fforts made and the steps taken by the 
Department to reach the public in the r ecent past to promote awareness among them 
about the peaceful usage and societal benefits  of atomic energy, it feels that the public 
apprehensions on the safety of nuclear installa tions, particularly, nuclear power plants as 
also possible fears of adverse impact on th eir traditional means of livelihood like fishing, 
biodiversity, health of work ers of Uranium mines and t hose living in the vicinity, 
environmental impact, etc. are strong and deep seeded.  These fears and apprehensions in 
the minds of the people arise mostly due to lack of communication, ignorance, gossips 
and rumour mongering.  Some amount of fear also comes out of the reported or perceived 
ill effects of radiation on th e people living nearby the nucl ear installations which are 
often exaggerated and blown out of proporti on by the media.  Fukushima accident, has 
further added to this fear psychosis and heightened the level of apprehensions.   
14.3  In such a complex scenario, what th e DAE needs to focus on, is to allay the 
apprehensions and misconceptions, harbour ed by the people against nuclear power 
projects by suitable, sustained and effective campaign with as wider reach as possible.  
Merely, organizing exhibitions and conducting seminars and producing some video films 
to cater to only a few lakhs of people would not have the desired impact.  The fact that 
during the last 40 years of commercial operati on of nuclear power plants in the country, 

not even a single, small incident has taken place needs to be emphatically and vigorously 
emphasised to the people.  If at all there are some genuine, legitimate concerns of the 
people as projected in the media from time to  time, the Department must instead of 
simply denying or ignoring them, proactivel y allay those fears a nd apprehensions by 
explaining to people in their own language a nd in a manner they would understand as to 
why their apprehensions or f ears are unfounded and that utmo st care has been taken to 
safeguard the interests of the public.   
14.4  The Committee, therefore, recommends that to earn the goodwill, trust and 
confidence of the people, the Department sh ould revisit the whole gamut of strategy 
and communication and evolve a long te rm programme and a llocate adequate 
budgetary resources for it.  The Committee also recommends that to take the 
authentic and authoritative me ssages to the public about sa fety and security of the 
nuclear power programmes, the Department should think in terms of constituting 
Area Standing Committees on public und erstanding of nuclear technologies 
consisting of reputed, respected and prominent public men of the area and scientists 
which should undertake the task to educate and enlighten the people of the area of 
the benefits of the project to them and allay their fears and apprehensions.  The 
Committee also recommends that even before a project is conceived, the 
Department should take stock of the li kely concerns of people and formulate 
suitable strategy/plan to address concern s and apprehensions of the people.  The 
Committee further recommends that ef forts on the lines suggested by the 
Committee should be initiated in and ar ound the areas where projects are pending 
for long due to public protests such as  Lambapur area in Andhra Pradesh and 
Kylleng-Pyndengsohiong Mawthabah (K PM Project) at Meghalaya or where 
projects are likely to come up.  The Co mmittee recognizes that efforts across the 
country in the areas of extension of  DAE societal outreach programme, 
implementation of appropriate mechan ism of communication through various 
media, and implementation of specific projects in different parts of the country will 
need funding under Non-Plan.  In view of this the Committe e recommends that 
DAE should be provided money to the exte nt of approx. hundred crores of rupees 
per year, based on annual requirement, to  set up a fund for public outreach and 
public information activities.   
 
15. Separate Reactors for Spin off Technologies  
 
15.1 The Committee enquired whethe r in view of a number of spin off, socially useful 
technologies developed by it, for use in the fi eld of medicine, indus tries, agriculture, 
processing of wastes, etc. popularity of whic h is growing tremendously and their demand 
is likely to see phenomenal gr owth in times to come, the Department of Atomic Energy 
proposes to set up separate reactors dedicate d exclusively for the a bove purpose so as to 
ensure seamless supply of radioisotopes fo r specific applications.  The Department 
replied that Dhruv Reactor in Trombay catered to most requirements of radioisotopes and 
as a short term measure provisions were al so being made in the existing and upcoming 
pressurized heavy water reactors for pr oduction of radioisotopes (Co-60).  The 
Department admitted that to meet the increasing requirement of various radioisotopes, a 
research reactor with large irra diation volume was essential.  It was also informed that a 
detailed project report for construction of  a 30 MW High Flux Research Reactor and a 
new Thermal Research Reactor of 125 MW ha s been prepared, construction of which is 
proposed to be initiated in the XII Five  Year Plan at BARC Campus, Vizag.  The 

Committee notes that the present demands fo r radioisotopes are being fully met by DAE 
but when the Dhruv reactor is shutdown for ma intenance, above radioisotopes need to be 
imported.  The Committee also finds that High Specific Activities Co-60 used for the 
treatment of Cancer by tele-therapy is not pr oduced in India due to the flux limitation in 
our nuclear reactors and hence is currently  being imported.  With the setting up of High 
Flux Reactor at Vizag the entire demand of Co-60 would be met.  The Committee is of 
the view that radioisotopes, which are bein g used in a number of socially useful 
technologies and any disrupti on in production of radioisot opes would adversely affect 
health, industry, agriculture sectors.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
construction work of High Flux Reacto rs proposed to be undertaken at 
Visakhapatnam needs to be put on fast trac k and all out efforts should be made to 
ensure its completion in the shortest possible time by devising a time schedule.   
 
16.  Tata Memorial Centre  
 
16.1 Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), a Grants-i n-aid Institution under the Department of 
Atomic Energy, comprises of Tata Memorial  Hospital and The Advanced Centre for 
Treatment, Research and Education in Canc er (ACTREC).  Diagnosis, treatment and 
research in Cancer as well as training and education to provide the highest standard of 
patient care form the core mandate of TMC.  It has established itself as an internationally 
well recognized cancer treatment instit ution and has a number of national and 
international accolades to its credit.  On an average, TMC handles in a year fifty thousand 
new patients and three lakhs fifty thousand follow up cases.   It has su cceeded in 
developing the capability of saving thousand of lives in India and even abroad at a 
minuscule cost of Rs. One hundred only.  Indigenously manufactured Telecobalt 
Machine ‘Bhabhatron-II’ in c ooperation with BARC has so fa r treated sixteen thousand 
patients.  TMC contributes to more than sixty per cent of national oncology human 
resources in the country.  It is also r unning a number of programmes to cater to the 
requirements of Cancer treatment through out reach programmes, running Mobile Cancer 
Screening & Urban static scr eening Centres, Cancer regist ries at identified sites, 
undertaking population based Cancer scr eening and epidemiology as preventive 
oncology, etc.  The Committee has been informed that to further strengthen the required 
infrastructure for Cancer treatment, the Deptt. proposes to establish two new 
Hospitals/Centres – one at Vizag, Andhra Prades h and the other at Chandigarh in Punjab 
and support Dr. B. Borooah Cancer Institute,  Guwahati, Assam and Tata Medical Centre, 
Kolkata.  Besides, the Depart ment is also running a National  Cancer grid for integration 
of service, research and education in Cancer for India.  
 
16.2 While, the Committee appreciates the tremendous efforts put in by the DAE in the 
area of Cancer, it feels that much more needs to be done to keep pace with the rapid and 
ever increasing incidence of Cancer in the county.  Cancer has started assuming alarming 
proportions in our country aff licting the poor, rural populace and even those not in the 
habit of consuming tobacco.  The poor and ev en the middle class people from the rural 
and urban areas are the worst sufferer, as they find themselves unable to afford the 
prohibitive and deterrent cost of  reliable and timely treatment mostly available in private 
hospitals.  In such a scenario patients from all over the country look towards TMC as the 
best and the only option/ alternative.   
 
16.3 The Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), therefor e, needs to rise to the occasion and try 
its level best to meet the expectations of the poor and the needy.  The Committee believes 
that TMC has the potential to do this and reso urce constraint is not coming in the way of 

its extension activities because  despite repeated query abou t the funds allocated to the 
Centre being sufficient or otherwise, th e Department did not come out with the 
categorical demand for additional resources.  The Committee expresses its anguish over 
the fact that as against the Plan allocation of Rs. 77.95 Cror es at the BE Stage in the year 
2012-13, TMC has revised Plan allocation of Rs. 31.00 Crores and worst, it was not able 
to incur even a single penny upto January, 2013.  Out of the total allocation both Plan, as 
well as, Non-Plan of Rs. 248.14 Crores, on ly an amount of Rs. 162.43 Crores was 
expected to be utilised upto January, 2013.  Th is sorry state of affairs, the Committee 
feels stands in a stark contrast to the aspi rations, expectations an d requirements of the 
people of the country which Centres of reput e and excellence like TMC are expected to 
fulfill.  The Committee takes a very serious view on the matter that the approved outlay 
has been allowed to go waste and ultimately lapse in such a manner.  When the 
Committee enquired about the reas ons for reduction in alloca tion at the RE Stage, the 
replies were – approval was still awaited fo r the establishment of Cancer Hospital in 
Vizag; delay in receipt of appr oval for project titled Advan ced Facilities for diagnostics 
and services; advanced facilities for cancer research and nuclear medicines; delay in 
construction activity for the project “Centre for Cancer epidemiology”, etc.  The 
Committee notes that there has been undue delay in the approval of plan projects by 
the Planning Commission practically rulin g out the possibility of making any 
significant expenditure under new plan pr ojects in the financial year 2012-13.  The 
Committee is of the view that the procedur al aspects ought to have been handled 
better and a proactive approach adopted to get the desired results which sadly was 
lacking.  The Committee also feels that considering the very large number of 
projects as well as their higher value, Secretary, DAE and the Atomic Energy 
Commission should be delegated enhanced financial powers for approval of projects 
in an expeditious and efficient manner.   
 
16.4  The Committee is, however, happy to note that this year budgetary allocation for 
TMC has been substantially increased in compar ison to that of the last year.  The total 
allocation, i.e., both Plan and Non-Plan ha s gone up from Rs. 248.14 Crores at the BE 
Stage in 2012-13 to Rs. 476.04 Crores this year , which is almost the double.  There has 
been a substantial increase  in the Plan allocation which has gone up from Rs. 77.95 
Crores in 2012-13 to Rs. 271.78 Crores in 2013-14.  But, at the same time, the 
Committee feels that this enhanced allocation can be able to do good or deliver, provided 
it is fully utilised.  The Committee feels that TMC must see its responsibilities 
through the prism of those who are sufferi ng from the dreaded and deadly disease 
of Cancer, but has nobody to come to their rescue or their succour.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department must ensure that the enhanced 
allocation is not only fully utilised in ex panding facilities and services but should 
also do so efficiently and quickly so that it could present a sound case for additional 
resources at RE Stage.   
 
16.5  The Committee takes a v ery serious view of the evasive, vague and casual 
reply to the Question as to whether TM C had any coordination / cooperation with 
the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, the nodal agency for treatment of Cancer.  
What was said was that TMC were the expe rt advisor to the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare for developing of the Nation al Cancer Institute in Jharjhar, Delhi.  
The Committee feels that since Cancer treatm ent is not the primary mandate of the 
Department of Atomic Energy but has come as a spin off technology with the 
Department and the Department is helping the Ministry of Health & Family 

Welfare by providing economical and eff ective Cancer treatment, it recommends 
that the Department of Atomic Energy must  partner with the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare – to achieve the rapi d expansion of quality diagnostics and 
treatment facilities of Cancer at affordable  rates so as to cover the entire populace 
of the country in a time bound manner.  Th is will help the spread of know-how and 
expertise available in Tata Memorial Ce ntre (TMC) across the country through the 
larger reach, in the health care field, of th e Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  
The Committee also recommends that the proposed establishment of Cancer 
Hospital in Vizag, Chandigarh and creation of infrastructure at other places, must 
be expeditiously completed in a given time  frame, so that their benefits start 
reaching the needy at the earliest.  Th e Committee further recommends that the 
Department must focus its attention on more and more research in the field of 
preventive oncology so that the incidence of Cancer could be contained.   
 
17.  Establishments/Installations of Atomic Energy in the States 
 
17.1 The Committee was informed that the Department of Atomic Energy has 107 
installations spread across all over the country almost in  all the States, providing benefit 
to the entire country.  The Department, through a map also apprised the Committee about 
the locations of the atomic energy establishm ents in India.  Wh ile acknowledging the far 
and wide presence of atomic energy establishments in the country, the Committee 
pointed out that spread of nuclear installati ons was not uniform in all the States of the 
country with only token  presence in norther n States particularly in bigger States like 
Bihar and Uttar Pradesh considered backwa rd and less developed.  The Department, 
however, in reply to a question stated that n ecessary steps were being taken to establish 
its facilities in other parts of the country in future.  When the Committee emphasised on 
the need of setting up of some establishment in  the North-Eastern States and Bihar, so as 
to provide the people of these States also th e benefits that atomic energy installations 
bring with them by way of neighbourhood welfare programmes under which welfare 
measures in the areas of health; educa tion; investment unde r Corporate Social 
Responsibility within a radius of 5 Kms. of the establishment etc. are undertaken.  As the 
incidence of Cancer was very high in this re gion as compared to the other regions of the 
country, the Committee wanted to know the steps taken by the Department in this 
direction.  The Director, Ta ta Memorial Centre responde d by saying that for North-
Eastern States two kinds of things had b een done.  One was extending whole hearted 
support – technical, financial, infrastructural,  etc. to Dr. B. Bor ooah Cancer Institute, 
Guwahati, so that patients from the northeas tern region did not ha ve to go beyond 
Guwahati.  Secondly, the Department was r unning 9 population based Cancer registries 
to find out as to why the incidence of Can cer was high and what type of Cancer was 
predominant in that region.  He further added th at prevalence of Cancer of gallbladder in 
that region was unique as it wa s not found anywhere in the wo rld except Chile.  Efforts 
were being made to trace out the reasons which caused this type of Cancer.  With regard 
to the arrangement for Cancer treatment under the aegis of TMC being made in Bihar, he 
informed that a delegation had visited Patna last month to assess the facilities that existed 
there and within a year, some arrangement woul d be put in place.  It was also informed 
that the State Government of Uttar Prades h had also invited TMC to advice on making 
some arrangements for Cancer treatment in  Lucknow or Kanpur and that opinion had 
already been given to them through a vision document. 
 

17.2 The Committee has been given to unders tand that as per a study conducted by 
National Cancer Registry Programme under th e Indian Council of Medical Research, 
eastern U.P. and flood planes of Bihar cove ring large areas, are the stretches where 
incidence of Cancer of Kidney, Food pipe, Pros tate, Liver, Urinary Bladder and skin is a 
national high because of reckless and relentless toxic industrial discharge such as arsenic; 
fluoride; chromium and other heavy metals, in to the River Ganga.  As per a news report, 
of every one lakh people surveyed, 20 to 25 people were found to be Cancer patients.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the gravity of the situation, 
which in all likelih ood may aggravate in time to come, the Department should 
seriously think of opening Cancer Registries in Patna and at a location to be decided 
in U.P. to assess the severity of the pr oblem and identify those suffering from 
Cancer.  The Committee also recommends that in order to provide cheap and 
affordable treatment in the vicinity, the Department should as a short-term 
measure, start a Cancer Centre under handholding scheme in the State Government 
Hospital, i.e., Indira Gandhi Institute, Patn a within one year as assured, but in the 
long run a full-fledged extension of Ta ta Memorial Centre should be started in 
AIIMS, Patna preferably in the XII Five Year  Plan itself.  Base d on the response of 
Govt. of Uttar Pradesh decision on starti ng cancer treatment facilities at Lucknow 
or Kanpur should also be taken expeditiously.   
18. Popularization of Spin off Technologies  
18.1 The Committee is aware that Departme nt of Atomic Energy has developed a 
number of spin off technologies which have the potential to serve the society and the 
people in numerous ways – keep the environm ent clean and healthy; help the people get 
safe water to drink; ameliorate lot of farmers by making them available high yielding and 
disease resistant crop varieties; help farm ers preserve and protect their agricultural 
produce for longer period apart from  those relevant in the field of healthcare, etc.  But it 
remains a matter of concern that despite th e Department having such socially useful 
technologies their benefits are only trickling down slowly to the society and the targeted 
groups.  This is mainly because the Departme nt has not made any proactive efforts to 
popularize and propagate them.  The Committee had in its 222 nd Report emphasised on 
the need to create a separate agency for popul arization of all these socially beneficial 
technologies but the Department  in its Action Taken Note le t the matter re st by saying 
that Board of Radiation and Isotopes Tec hnology (BRIT) had already been created in 
1989 for popularization and marketing of social ly beneficial tec hnologies under nuclear 
medicine and healthcare.  When the Committ ee enquired about the steps taken in this 
direction, the Department of Atomic Energy, although, gave a detailed account of various 
technologies developed by diffe rent R&D Centres, it still did not come out with the 
details of the activities undertaken for thei r popularization.  The Committee is happy to 
learn that the Department ha s been able to transfer 19 different technologies to the 
entrepreneurs in the year 2009, 20 in 2010 and 10 & 35 in the year 2011 & 2012 
respectively.  In the Year 2013, 6 tec hnologies had been transferred by 11 th February, 
2013.  The Committee, however, is not, at all,  satisfied with the pace of progress of 
technology transfer and feels that it needs to  be intensified and expedited because it 
is only through transfer that the benefi ts of technology reach the society.  The 
Committee understands that the Department of Atomic Energy had established an 
institute in the form of Board of Radi ation and Isotope Technology (BRIT) to 
transfer technologies relevant to medicine and healthcare, but it has not set up any 
such institutionalized mechan ism, for the technologies in the fields of agriculture, 

water purification, sludge hygienisation fo r treatment of municipal sewage, food 
irradiation, etc.  The Committee, there fore, recommends that the Department 
should create an institutional mechanism exclusively for popularization of these 
technologies on the lines of BRIT.  Beside s, for popularization and dissemination of 
technologies related to agriculture, the Depa rtment should also evolve an effective 
and potent mechanism of cooperation and coordination with the Central 
Agricultural Universities and the State Agri cultural Universities, so as to achieve 
effective dissemination of information on new seed varieties and other information 
relevant to the farmers.   
19. Integration of Spin-Off Technologies  with Related Schemes of Ministries
 
19.1 The Committee feels that yet anothe r effective way of successfully and 
adequately utilizing the socially beneficial technologies could be to  integrate them with 
the related programmes/schemes being run by di fferent Ministries/ Departments of Govt. 
of India.  All that the Department needs to do is to reach out to th e concerned Ministries/ 
Departments and to impress upon them to inte grate into their programmes/projects, these 
proven technologies.  For example, providing potable drinking water in rural and urban 
areas has turned out to be a formidable cha llenge for the Ministries of Rural and Urban 
Development/ Local Administra tion, etc.  Department of  Atomic Energy has proven 
technology for water purificati on and water desalination, which costs as less as 6 Paisa 
per liter.  This technology can easily be replicated at all those places facing safe potable 
water problems or where underground water is contaminated with arsenic or fluoride, etc. 
both in urban and rural areas of the country by getting it linked with Rural Water Mission 
and in the urban areas with the Urban Local Bodies.  Similarly, Department of Atomic 
Energy can help Ministry of Water Res ources draw a map of water hydrology by 
prospecting and locating availability of underground water with the help of Isotope 
Hydrology Technology readily available with them so that wa ter tapped from the surplus 
area could be channelised in the arid, pa rched and those areas that face drought like 
situation like the one being f aced in Maharashtra now.  This  way, the Department would 
also integrate the National Water Security Sy stem with the technologies available with it 
on a regular basis.   Likewise, the Sludge Hygienisa tion Research Irradiation (SHRI) 
technology can be integrated with the guidelin es laid down for Sewage Treatment Plants 
(STPs) by the CPCB so that, it could be  a certified & recommended technology for use 
by urban and local municipal bodies for sewage  treatment, which is also emerging as a 
major challenge in the urban areas of the c ountry.  This technology can also play a major 
role in the JNNURM Programme run by the Ministry of Urban Development, which has 
a component of sewage treatment.  The technology on food irradiation could be 
integrated with the programmes of the Minist ry of Food Processing Industries.  By doing 
all this, the Committee feels the Department w ould be able to disseminate its socially 
beneficial technologies in a big way and their benefits wo uld also reach easily to the 
people and the society.  This will also help the Department earn creditability and good 
will in the larger populace and clear the apprehensions/ misconceptions in the minds of 
the people towards atomic energy.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department must act on the lines being suggested by the Committee and initiate 
interaction with the concerned Ministries  to convince them of the relevance and 
efficacy of its technologies within a given time schedule.  It also recommends the 
Department to take all possible measures to take the technologies to the society as a 
technology lying in the labyrinth of laboratory or an institution is useless and 
meaningless.  Its real success lies in its wider & wider applications and use.   

 
20. Power Sector  
20.1 There is no gainsaying that  the fact that the Department of Atomic Energy has 
done commendable work covering wide ranging areas and has created wonderful 
infrastructural facilities for outstanding scientific work, but, somehow it has not been able 
to live to the expectation of  ensuring energy security to the country.  It has miserably 
failed thus far to emerge as a formidable, a lternative source of en ergy.  The country is 
still heavily dependent on thermal and hydr o power plants which have their own 
limitations and adverse consequence on the health of environment and ecology.  The 
share of nuclear in total energy generation is still hovering around 3.7 per cent with the 
total installed capacity of 4780 MW.  This capacity is expected to reach 10080 MW by 
the end of the XII Five Year Plan by progr essive addition of 5300 MW – 4 Pressurized 
Water Reactors (2X700) Kakrapar Atomic Power Plant in Gujarat and Rawatbhata 
Atomic Power Plant (2X700) in Rajasthan, one  Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) 
of 500 MW capacity at Kalpakkam, Tamilnadu expected to be made critical by 
September, 2014 and 2 Light Water Reactor s (2X100), Kudankulam, Tamilnadu which 
are at advanced stage of commissioning.  New sites of Gorakhpur in Haryana and Chutka 
in Madya Pradesh, in-principle approval for which was accorded in October, 2009 are 
also at various stages of development.  The Government has also accorded in-principle 
approval for setting up of nuclear power projects in Kudankulam (3&4) Tamilnadu; 
Jaitapur, Maharashtra; Chhaya Mithi Vrid i, Gujarat; Kovada, Andhra Pradesh and 
Haripur, West Bengal where pre-project activities have commenced.   
20.2  On being enquired by the Committee on the status of Nawada (Bihar) one of the 
prospective places identified for setting up of a nuclear power plant, the Department 
replied that a team of Nuclear Power Cor poration of India Ltd. (NPCIL) had gone very 
recently to Nawada, Rajauli for identification of sites for setting up of two units of 700 
MW capacity power plants there.  Initially, there was some requirement of water which 
was becoming a constraint and the proposal wa s withdrawn but with the recent initiative 
from the Govt. of Bihar once again to make water available and fulfill other conditions 
which are required for the site of a nuclear power plant, the process has started again.  
The Committee takes note of the informati on given by the Department and hopes that a 
decision regarding this site as a designate d location for Nuclear Power Plant would be 
taken shortly.   
20.3  The Committee finds that the projecti ons of the Department, particularly, 
regarding setting up of nuclear power plants ar e prone to slippage and are rarely adhered 
to.  Department of Atomic Energy, as per the XI Five Year Plan Mid-Term Appraisal 
document, envisaged starting work on 8 Units of 700 MW in the XI Five Year Plan.  But 
out of the proposed 8, work on 4 Units only coul d be started in the XI Five Year Plan.  
Similarly, as per the Mid-Term Appraisal document, the Fast Breeder Reactor at 
Kalpakkam was likely to be commissioned by  March, 2012, but no w the date of its 
commissioning has been extended to Septem ber, 2014.  The Committee is aware of the 
oddities, challenges and hurdles th at DAE had faced in the past , or is still facing, but the 
test of true ability, capability and conviction lies in overcoming these obstructions in the 
shortest possible time.  The Departme nt cannot go on repeating the grounds of 
technology denial and the t echnological challenges that th e Fast Breeder Reactor, 
Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (the second a nd the third stages of the nuclear power 
programme) being new, pose, etc.  The Department cannot abdicate itself of 
responsibilities for not being able to deliver in these areas.   

 
20.4  The Committee is constrained to observ e that the financial performance of the 
Department in respect of power sector has also been dismal and poor.  It f eels that there 
could be no plausible or convincing reason, whatsoever, to justify the expected utilisation 
upto January, 2013 of a meager amount of Rs . 5.72 Crores only, out of the BE and RE 
Budgetary Support of Rs. 998.27 Crores and Rs . 575.00 Crores respectiv ely for the year 
2012-13 for Power sector.   
20.5  The Committee is astonished to note  that BHAVINI which is shouldering the 
responsibility of building Fast Breeder Reactor has not been able to utilize even a single 
penny upto January, 2013, out of the Plan Head B.E. allocation of Rs. 536.67 Crores in 
2012-13.  The position prevailing in the y ears 2010-11 and 2011-12 was not any better.  
The actual utilisation of the Budgetary Support under Pl an Head had stood at Rs. 708.24 
Crores as against the BE allocation of Rs . 1848.00 Crores in the year 2010-11 while in 
the year 2011-12, the corres ponding figure was Rs. 875.00 Cror es as against Rs. 1609.00 
Crores.  The Committee also finds that th e Plan Head Budgetary Support for Power 
Sector over the years has been on the dec line, i.e., Rs. 1848.00 Crores in 2010-11 Rs. 
1609.00 Crores in 2011-12, Rs. 998.00 Crores in  2012-13 and Rs. 716.14 Crores in the 
current year.  The Committee feels that the above situation does not  present a healthy 
picture about the nuclear energy scenario  in the country and it is high-time the 
Department of Atomic Energy takes this decl ining trend as a wake up call to take some 
proactive measures for optimum  utilisation of allocated funds  or else a time may come 
when the funding to this sector would dry out.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department should galvanize its resources and intensify its efforts to ensure 
that the proposed power projects are co mpleted and commissioned well within the 
scheduled deadline, and to do this, the De partment must make optimum utilisation 
of the Budgetary Support extended to it for the purpose.  The Committee 
recommends that Department should seriously pay attention to the fact that country 
cannot endlessly wait for the nuclear energy to emerge as an alternative option.  As 
such, the Department should now do what is required to be done in this direction on 
utmost priority basis.   
21. Environmental Advisor for De partment of Atomic Energy
 
21.1 The Committee finds that a number of pr ojects of the Department of Atomic 
Energy mainly relating to Uranium projects are held up for want of environmental 
clearances.  The planned construction of Gogi Uranium Project in Karnataka and 
expansion of Tummalapall e Uranium Project in Andhra Pradesh are awaiting 
environmental clearance since 2011, despite pur suing this matter several times with the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests.  Several other projects get stuck up or delayed on the 
apprehensions of they being potential health hazard and result ultimately in public 
outrage & protest.  Sometimes, environm entalists also join the public opposing the 
proposed projects.  The Committee feels that  the Department needs to address these 
concerns sometimes genuine and mostly ap prehensions, in a more scientific and 
professional manner, so as not to allow it to take the shape and colour of the development 
versus environment safety.  In order to do this, the Committee feels that the Department 
should have an environmental advisor on the lines  of financial advisor in the Ministry of 
Finance, who would be involved in the proj ects from the very beginning and make a 
proactive analysis of likely environmental pr oblems.  This arrangement would help the 
Department get required environmental cleara nces from the Minist ry of Environment & 
Forests in a speedy manner and would al so go a long way in alleviating unfound 

apprehensions of the people and the envir onmentalists about the proposed projects.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should seriously think on 
this suggestion of the Committee and take appropriate action in the matter. 
22. Harish Chandra Research Institute, Allahabad  
22.1 The Harish Chandra Research Institute is one of the premier research Institutes in 
the country devoted to fundamental research in  the fields of Mathematic and Theoretical 
Physics.  When the Committee visited the In stitute at Allahabad in January, 2013, it was 
impressed with its prevailing academic envir onment and the dedicated team of scientists/ 
faculties.  One of the faculties, Prof. Ashoke Sen has become the first Indian scientist to 
be conferred with the prestigious The Fundamental Physics Prize, 2012 by Miler 
Foundation for string theory.   
22.2  The Committee finds that Harish Cha ndra Research Institute had got a total 
budgetary outlay of Rs. 37.21 Crores, Rs. 20.10 Crores under Plan head and Rs. 17.11 
Crores under Non-Plan Head at the BE leve l in the year 2012-13.  However, the Plan 
allocation of Rs. 20.10 Crores was reduced to Rs . 5.00 Crores at the RE stage.  When the 
Committee enquired about the reasons for the sharp reduction in the approved outlay at 
the RE Stage, the Department informed that this was due to delay in construction 
activities of the new confer ence centre under the Project civil and infrastructure 
development, non-receipt for the sanction for the new project “Advanced Research 
Facilities for Theoretical Physics”, etc.   The Committee is happy to note that BE 
allocation under Plan Head this year has gone up from Rs. 20.10 Crores in the year 2012-
13 to Rs. 27.12 Crores.  The Co mmittee feels that such a prestigious institute, dedicated 
and devoted to the cause of Physics & Math ematics and capable of  making the country 
proud of its achievements fully deserves all necessary assistance from the Department.  
The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy must 
render all the help required by the Institute.   It also recommends that efforts should 
not only be made to meet it s requirements but efforts shou ld also be made to grant 
expeditious sanction for the advanced resea rch facilities for theoretical physics, so 
that, the Institute could be able to excel further in pursuit of its objectives.   
23. Atomic Minerals Dir ectorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) & 
Uranium  Corporation of India Ltd. (UCIL) 
23.1 Atomic Minerals Directorate is entrus ted with the task to carry out survey, 
prospecting and exploration of atomic minerals requir ed for the nuclear power 
programme of the country.  It also carries out site selection for the nuclear power reactors 
and waste disposals.  Uranium Corporation of  India Ltd. (UCIL) undertakes the task to 
design and construct underground mines, or e processing plants and other related 
facilities.  The activities of these two Ins titutes are thus closely interlinked with each 
other.  Budgetary Support for Atomic Minera ls Directorate (AMD) extends to two Major 
heads, i.e., Major Head 5401 which pertains to Research & Development and the Major 
Head 4861 relating to Minerals  Sector.  While the Plan Budgetary allocation for AMD 
under R&D and Minerals Sectors were Rs. 51.64 Crores and 51.15 Crores respectively at 
the BE Stage in 2012-13, they came down to Rs. 44.00 Cores and Rs. 25.00 Crores 
respectively at the RE Stage.  When th e Committee enquired about the reasons for 
reduction in allocation at the RE Stage, th e Department stated that non-receipt of 
approvals/clearances for airborne survey by At omic Minerals Directorate for Exploration 
and Research (AMD) and National Geophysi cal Research Institu te (NGRI) and the 
slowing in contract drilling due to logistic problems in Meghalaya, technical problems in 

southern Cuddapah Basin, social economic cons traints in Jharkhand, etc. resulted in 
reduction of RE Budget in 2012-13.   
23.2  The Committee finds that the total Plan  Outlay for Atomic Minerals Directorate 
has come down to Rs. 100.52 Crores this year as against the Rs. 102.79 Crores at BE 
level in 2012-13.  Now coming to the Uranium Corporation of India Ltd., the Committee 
finds that both the Plan and Non-Plan allocations of Rs. 216.00 Crores and 251.00 Crores 
respectively got reduced to Rs. 18.50 Crores ea ch at the RE Stage.  The reduction in the 
allocation was attributed to non-receipt of  environmental clearances for the Uranium 
Project at Gogi and the e xpansion of Tummalapalle Project.  When the Committee 
wanted to know the reasons for reduction in  the Plan allocation in  the year 2013-14 for 
UCIL as compared to the BE allocation of the last year which works out to the extent of 
Rs. 71.00 Crores, it was stated that while the Department was making best of its efforts to 
increase the exploration of uranium resources in the country but the quality of domestic 
Uranium ore was very poor in terms of percen tage of Uranium present in it.  While the 
domestic Uranium contained as low as 0.03 to 0.04 per cent of Uranium in comparison to 
the international quality where the percentage we nt upto 1 to 3 per cent.  This resulted in 
substantial increase in the price of domestic  Uranium after processing the ore which was 
close to Rs. 18000 per Kg., while the price of  imported Uranium worked out to around 
Rs. 6000 per Kg., almost one third of the domes tic price.  It was further added that the 
overall policy, therefore, was to import Ur anium in a brisk manner as compared to 
emphasising on domestic production of Uranium.   This was also being done because 
ultimately whatever available within the coun try was available to us  forever and so long 
as we were able to get it, we should do so.   
23.3  While the Committee agrees with the contention of the Department to the extent 
that the import of Uranium is economical it being cheaper, however it feels that domestic 
development of uranium mines as well as processing of Uranium ores by UCIL must also 
go side by side not only to enable faster development of the nucle ar energy sector, but 
also to keep ready to brace any eventualitie s of disruption or denial of Uranium by 
international community at any given stage.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department of Atomic Energy should not ignore or go slow on the 
indigenous prospecting exploration mini ng and processing of Uranium simply 
because of the fact that imported Uraniu m is much cheaper or is, presently, being 
made available by the international communit y.  Priority must continue to be given 
to the development of domestic Uranium and devising of means of cheaper and 
more efficient extractions of Uranium from the ores and adequate financial 
resources must be made available to Atom ic Minerals Directorate and Uranium 
Corporation of India Ltd., more so, because the gestation period of mining typically 
requires 10 years and any incidence of su dden disruption or de nial of imported 
Uranium can put us in precarious situation.    
24.  Nuclear Agriculture 
 
24.1 Vagaries of monsoon, poor precipitat ion, scattered rainfall, diminishing 
underground water table, faltering irrigation fac ilities, receding ecological flow of rivers, 
etc. caused due to climate change have put tremendous pressure on our poor and marginal 
farmers particularly of the wheat & paddy gr owing States of the country.  In such a 
situation, it becomes imperati ve to develop such varietie s of wheat & rice which could 
withstand biotic as well abiotic stress.  Although, the Department of Atomic Energy, 
under its Project Nuclear Agriculture is work ing in this area and has tested a rice 
involving mutant which was found to be high yielding and has also tested early mutants 

of Cv. C306 in wheat, the Committee desires that research & development activities in 
this area need to be further intensified so as to come out with viable solutions at the 
earliest.  Yet another area, in which, the Co mmittee would like the Department to focus 
its attention on, is preservation & prolonging the shelf life of onion and potato through its 
irradiation technology to provide relief to fa rmers belonging to different parts of our 
country – Punjab, Maharashtra, West Bengal,  Bihar, etc. who are often heard to be 
throwing their onion and potato products on roads because they do not have access to any 
technology to keep them for longer period nor do they get remunerative price during the 
peak season.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy 
should explore the possibilities to start wo rking in this area, in a mission mode and 
come out with viable solutions in a time bound manner.  
24.2  The Committee hopes that the Departme nt of Atomic Energy would give due 
considerations to the observations and recommendations of the Committee and try 
to do its best to take such actions/ steps required to given them the practical shape.  
The Committee is confident that as outlin ed in its outcome budget the Department 
of Atomic Energy would make XII Five  Year Plan more oriented towards 
programme with objectives rather th an spending efforts in building 
infrastructure/equipment facilities that may exist elsewhere.  The Committee also 
hopes that the delivery of output by the Department during the current Five Year 
Plan would be more than what is commensurate with the resources utilized.

INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Science and Technology was established in 1971 to formulate 
and implement Science and Technology polic ies, identify, and promote "frontline" 
research in science and technology infrastr ucture. The Ministry ha s three Departments, 
namely Department of Science & Tec hnology, Department of Biotechnology and 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Re search. Through Department of Science and 
Technology, the Ministry coordinates intra- governmental and international cooperation 
and provides funding for domestic institutions and research programs. The Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Re search is a technology tran sfer organization, and the 
Department of Biotechnology, runs a number of developmental laboratories. 
2. The following constitute the mandate of DST:-  
 Formulation of policy statements a nd guidelines on Science and Technology 
(S&T). 
 Promotion of new areas of scientific research. 
 Co-ordination of inter-Departmental S&T efforts. 
 Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions. 

 International S&T Co-operation. 
 Support high quality research in autonom ous bodies where specialization ranges 
from advanced medical research materials to astronomy. 
 Catalyzing S&T interaction in societal  programmes, and entrepreneurship 
development.  
 Science popularization, communicati on and S&T Management Information 
System. 
 Promotion of Commercialization of home grown technology. 
 Support to technology development prog rammes, technology information and 
assessment. 
 Providing services in the areas of: 
(i) Surveying & Mapping  
(ii) Technology Development and Application  
3. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP 
3.1 The Department of Science & Technology is the nodal Department of the 
Ministry of Science and Technology.  The Or ganizational Structure of the Department 
has evolved over the years to re spond quickly to the issues relating to the promotion and 
development of Science & Technology in the country. Broadly, the organisational set up 
of the Department has been divided into Autonomous Institutes, Scientific Groups, 
Technology Development Board, Scientific Services besides the Administration and 
Integrated Finance divisions. Ther e are 19 Autonomous Institutes and 5 
Science/Engineering Professional bodies wh ich are working in diverse areas for the 
promotion of Science and Technology. In addition, one new autonomous body viz. 
National Centre for Molecular Material  Rese arch, Thiruvanathapuram has been recently 
set up and National Innovation Foundation, Ahmedabad which was earlier a ‘Corpus 
Funded’ Financial Institute  has been taken over by the Department  as fully funded 
autonomous Research Institute. The Scientific Groups inter-alia consists of the Science 
& Engineering Research Council (SERC), Na tional Council for Science & Technology 
Communication (NSCTC), National Resources  Data Management System (NRDMS), 
International Division, Nati onal Entrepreneurship Board (NEB), National Science and 
Technology Management Information System (NSTMIS). The Scientific Services has 
two subordinate offices, viz., National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation 
(NATMO) and Survey of India (SoI) under its administrative control. 
3.2 The detailed budget allocation of the De partment of  Science and Technology, for 
the year 2013-2014 was considered by the Department-related Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment & Forests on the 16
th April, 2013.

4.3 The Committee notes that while the Planning Commission has accepted in toto  
the outlays projected by the Department pertaining to Modernisation of Mapping 
Organisation (SoI and NATMO), it has also substantially increased allocation to Drugs & 
Pharmaceutical Research by 100 crores.  For Science and Engineering Research Board, 
the approved outlay has been phenomenally in creased to   3796 cror es as against the 
projected demand of  only  50 crores. 
4.4 The Committee, however, finds that ther e is a gap of  9964.00 Crores between the 
total demand projected by the Department and the outlay approved. The Committee notes 
that allocation to the Department has been toned down by near ly 32% and feels that such 
drastic reduction in the alloca tion may lead to re-prioritiz ation of allocations among the 
different schemes by the Department specially for such important and crucial schemes as 
Research and Development Support, Mega  Facilities for Basic Research, Disha 
Programme for Women in Science, etc.  
4.5 Considering India’s aspirations to pos ition itself among the top five global 
scientific powers by 2020 and the immense potential of science &technology for societal 
benefits, the Committee is of the opinion that adequate funds should be allocated to the 
Department.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the Planning Commission 
should provide additional funds, if so required by the Department. 
5. TREND OF UTILISATION IN THE LAST THREE YEARS 
5.1 A comparison of the B.E., R.E allocation made and actual expenditure incurred by 
the Department for the years 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2012-13 is given below:

5.2 After an examination of B.E. and R.E.  allocations vis-à-vis actuals for the 
financial year 2010-11, 2011- 12 and 2012-13 (up to 22 nd February, 2013) of the 
Department of Science & Technology, it is found that underutilisation of approved outlay 
is a chronic problem with the Department.  
5.3 In the financial year 2010-11, the total a llocation including Plan and Non-Plan at 
B.E. was   2376.50 Crores and R.E.  2376.95 Crores but actua l utilisation by the 
Department was only 2280.77 Crores which is  96.18 Crores less than the RE

was to the extent of   2521.66 Crores which is  93.58 Crores less than the RE

5.4 In comparison to this, for the year 2012- 13, out of the total Plan BE outlay of

5.5 The Committee observes that the compara tive statement depicted on the previous 
page clearly indicates that though funds had been allocated to the Department, it failed to 
optimally utilise them.  This also provides the Planning Commission with an easy excuse 
to resort to cut in the proposed demand of the Department.  
5.6 The Department must keep this fact in mind that budgetary resources are very 
scarce and a priority is given to the scien tific Departments in th e hope of better use of 
funds, both qualitative and quantitative. It  is, noteworthy, that Department’s 
underutilisation of allocated resources for thr ee years in a row does not present a healthy 

picture of the Department.  It ra ther reflects upon its performance.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that every possible e ffort should be made to utilise the 
budgetary allocation optimally.  The Co mmittee finds that the phenomenon of 
underutilisation persists despite the claim of the Department of having a very sound 
and robust monitoring mechanism.  The Co mmittee is constrained to observe that 
the monitoring mechanism of the Department  appears to be strong, on paper only, 
as it has failed to produce satisfactory and desired result of ensuring full utilisation 
of allocated resources, and therefore recommends that the Department should 
further strengthen its monitoring mechanism and make it more robust to ensure full 
and effective utilisation of allocated funds.   
6. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2013-14 
6.1 The Committee has been informed that the Department has been allocated a Plan

When the Committee enquired as to whether the funds allocate d were sufficient to carry 
out the activities of the Department, it was st ated that the allocation for the Department 
had been kept at the BE 2012-13 level fo r its on-going activitie s and commitments. 
Further, some of the programmes under the Technology Development and programme for 
Climate Change and Public Private Partnershi p (PPP) for R&D were likely to suffer due 
to insufficient fund allocation.  
6.3 The Committee feels that such  cuts would lead to shor tage of resources and may 
adversely affect the progress of some of th e programmes. The Committee, further, notes 
that these disturbing cuts have been impos ed when the new Science, Technology and 
Innovation Policy, 2013 has been launched with much fanfare.  While on one hand, the 
Government has given a healthy sign of promoting science and innovations in the 
country, it had not shown faith on the scien tific Departments like DST on the other by 
imposing cuts on its proposed allocations.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that adequate funds should be made available to the Depa rtment at the RE stage by 
the Planning Commission based on its requirements.   
7. Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013 
7.1 Department of Science and Technol ogy is primarily entrusted with the 
responsibility to formulate Policies, their implementation, identification and promotion of 
thrust areas of research in different sect ors of science and technology and assessment of 
science and technology activities in the country.   
7.2 The Department formulated Technology Policy Statement in 1983 and two 
decades later, Science and Technology Policy was introduced in 2003.  New Science 
Technology and Innovation Policy has been initia ted this year by the Department which 

was released by the Prime Minister at the 100 th Session of Indian Science Congress at 
Kolkata.  Some of the key elements of the policy include:- 
 Promoting the spread of scientific tempers amongst all sections of society. 
 Enhancing skill for applications of science among the young from all social strata. 
 Establishing would class infrastructure for R&D for gaining global leadership in 
some select frontier areas of science. 
 Positioning India among the top five global scientific powers by 2020 and 
 Fostering resource-optimized, cost-effective innovations across size and 
technology domains.  
7.3 When the Committee enquired about th e performance of Science & Technology 
Policy 2003, the Department stated that Science and Technology Policy 2003 stressed on 
raising the quality of life of the people of the country, particularly  of the disadvantaged 
sections of society, by creating wealth fo r all; making India globally competitive; 
utilising natural resources in a sustaina ble manner, protecting the environment and 
ensuring national security, etc.   
7.4 The Department further informed that  since the enunciation of the Science & 
Technology Policy 2003 several new programmes and schemes have been introduced to 
vigorously foster scientific research in universities and other academic, scientific and 
engineering institutions; to attract the brightest young persons to pursue careers in science 
and technology by conveying a sense of excite ment concerning the advancing frontiers, 
and by creating suitable employment opportunities for them.  
7.5 The Department also informed that th e industrial R&D investment grew by 250% 
and the sales by 200% between 2005 and 201 0.  The gross budgetary support for the 
science and technology sector has significantly  increased during the last decade.  The 
impact of such increase is becoming evident.    Another significant achievement of STI 
Policy, 2003 is now India ranks ninth globally in the number of scientific publications 
and 12th in the number of patents filed.  Th e Composite Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 
global share has increased from 1.8% in 2001 to 3.5% in 2011. 
7.6 Focus Areas of STI Policy, 2013 
 The main advantage of STI Policy,  2013 over Science & Technology Policy,2003 
is that the former seeks to integrate innova tion, as an instrument of Policy which was 
hitherto not  accorded due importance,  with Science & Technology.  Science, technology 
and innovation can though exist separately on their own in disconnected spaces, it is their 
integration that leads to new value cr eation.  Innovation thus implies Science & 
Technology 
Based solutions that are successfully deployed in the economy or society. 
7.7 The Department informed that with th e STI Policy, 2013, the Department’s focus 
would be on  preparing statement for aspi rational goals; to focus on innovation for 
application of knowledge for wealth and va lue creation; to adopt evidence-based 
approaches for policy development; to enrol stakeholders through wi de consultations; to 
focus on Public Private Partnership for attractin g private sector investment into R&D; to 
strike a balance in R&D priorities- excellence and relevance; to approach by integrating 
science, research and  innovation system for high technology  led path as a specific policy 
goal; and to include measurements and accountability as indicators for investments. 
7.8 Department further added that the Gove rnment has taken some other important 
measures to encourage Research and Devel opment in the country namely: induction of 
new and attractive fellowships; strengthe ning infrastructure for Research and 
Development (R&D); and encouraging public-private R&D partnerships, etc.  

7.9 The Committee understands that STI Policy, 2013 is a Policy document which 
draws a broad roadmap which inter-alia includes use of science & technology for the 
benefit of people and advancement of India as a global scientific power.  These are 
undoubtedly noble objectives but to make them laudable the Department needs to pursue 
them with all vigour and earnestness in order to ensure that they do not remain  only on 
paper but are translated into reality.  
7.10 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the key goals enshrined in the 
Policy document should be realised within the given timeframe particularly the goal 
of positioning India amongst the top five global scientific powers by 2020 and the 
Department must make all out efforts to achieve these goals.

10. STATE OF R&D INVESTMENTS    
10.1 The Department of Science and T echnology is running four schemes for 
extending support for infrastructure st rengthening of R&D namely: Fund for 
Infrastructure Strengthening of S&T (FIST), Special packages for regional balancing of 
FIST reach, Consolidation of University Research, Innovation and Excellence (CURIE)

Besides, DST under bilateral S& T cooperation agreements also  supports institutions that 
compete through quality proposals for establis hing science-bridges with institutions in 
other countries such as United Kingdom.   
10.2 As regards the state of R&D investments, the Department stated that, if India has 
to emerge as one of the top five knowledge powers in the world by 2020, right sizing of 
R&D investments while simultaneously br oadening the R&D base with stronger 
participation of the private sector would be necessary.  
10.3 When the Committee enquired about the reasons behind insufficient growth in 
R&D expenditure from the last Scien ce & Technology Policy 2003, the Department’s 
reply was vague. It stated, “Gross Expenditure  into R&D has gone up considerably since 
the enunciation of the Science & Technology Polic y 2003.  Whereas the Gross 
Expenditure into R&D as of 2003 was estimated at US $ 12 billion (after adjustments to 

Purchase Power Parity), currently the corre sponding figures are mo re than double of 
2003 investments.’’  
10.4 It is evident from the reply that no cl ear cut figure for R&D investment in 2013 
was provided by the Department. In absence of current figures of Gross Expenditure into 
R&D the Committee finds it difficult to quantify the achievement of STP 2003. 
10.5 The Department stated that though Indi a’s R& D investment as percentage of 
GDP may seem small in terms of Gross Expend iture, there is a significant increase in 
investment since the coming up of  Scien ce & Technology Policy, 2003. Benefits of such 
investments are becoming evident with improve ments in relative ranking of India with 
respect to publications from 13 in 2003 to 9
th in 2010 and perhaps better than 9 th in 2012 
and from 25th in patent generation in 2003 to XII in 2010.  
10.6 Informing about efforts made for increas ing R&D Expenditure in the country, the 
Department added that it aims at increasing the total R&D expenditure as percentage of 
GDP to 2 percent by the end of XII Five Year Plan period from the current level of less 
than 1 percent. Actual expenditure of the G overnment in real terms is more than double 
during the XI Five Year Plan period in comparison to the  X Five Year Plan.  Allocation 
for the six science Departments for the XII Five  Year Plan is about 160 percent of the XI 
Five Year Plan allocation. These trends repr esent a significant increase in deployment of 
resources considering the overall resources of the country. The Government proposes to 
achieve the targeted goal during the XII Five  Year Plan period through various measures 
such as policy advocacy, increase in invest ment in R&D including industry and strategic 
sectors, expansion of basic science infras tructure, aligning S&T to development needs 
like food and health care, evolving new models of public-private partnership in scientific 
research, encouraging international collaborat ion etc. in the whole development process 
in that particular region.  
10.7 Of late, concerns have also been raised  to increase private s ector investment in

10.8 The Committee enquired about the effort s made by the Department for enhancing 
the contribution of the private sector in R & D. In response thereto, Department stated 
that the private sector engagement in R&D is presently small except in a few sectors such 
as pharmaceuticals, fine chemicals, and automotives mainly due to small size of the 
Indian industrial firms, hi gh risks, low appropriability  and disincentives created by high 
transaction costs and weak R&D fiscal support. 
10.9 The Department informed that in order to address few of these bottlenecks and to 
encourage the private sector to take up and st ep up its R&D activities a number of steps  
have been taken by them to address the concern which aim to enhance the contribution of 
the private sector for instan ce enlarging R&D base and invi te greater investments using 
global data base; PPP model for R&D for pub lic and social good, preparation of a 

concept note with regard to the PPP in R& D and clean energy   as a part of sub-
committee of PM’s Council on Trade and Indus try leaders, to study and assess the 
investments of private sector in R&D sect or; devising new modes and mechanisms to 
draw a comprehensive picture of R&D landscape in India by way of making more precise 
estimates of national investments in the R& D that includes the  R&D contributions of 
MNCs as well. 
10.10 The Committee feels that India is lagging far behind ot her countries of the world 
in respect of R & D contribution made by the Private sector.  In comparison to developed 
countries of the world, India’s R&D funding from non-government sector is abysmally 
low.  Even in comparison to our neighbour ing country China, we  lag far behind. The 
percentage contribution of private sector and public sect or to R&D contribution in India 
& China is nearly in reverse order.  In Ch ina private sector cont ribution is nearly 70 
percent of R&D expenses while in India it is Government which makes 75 to 80 percent 
contribution.   
10.11 The Committee feels that in order to e nhance investment in R&D, the private 
sector’s contribution needs to be significantly augmented.  The Committee had in its 
223
rd report emphasised on the need to enhan ce private sector contribution to R&D 
by offering incentives, forming partnership,  etc.  The Department in their Action 
Taken Replies endorsed the view of the Co mmittee but the desired result still eludes 
us. The Committee feels that somewhere we have  failed in our efforts to woo private 
sector and not much has been achieved even in the second year of the XII Five Year 
Plan period.  
10.12 The Committee recommends that Ministry  must devise innovative ways to 
substantially increase private sector investme nt in R&D in order to make it at par 
with the investment of private sector in  R&D in other develo ped countries.  The 
Government may even consider making cont ribution of the private sector in R&D 
mandatory taking a cue from South Korean experience which reversed South 
Korean government’s burden in Science & t echnology Sector in a decade with a 
series of laws.  The Committee, further, recommends that Government should, in all 
situations ensure that investment in R&D gets enhanced to atleast 2% of Gross 
Domestic Product at the earliest so as to realise the goal of becoming a scientific 
super power by 2020.

a) Promotion of University Research and Scientific Excellence" (PURSE):-  PURSE 
is a Research Incentive Grant program for re juvenation of research at the University 
Sector initiated by the Department of Science and Technology.

papers/journals.

grant scheme was designed and awards were presented by the Hon'ble Prime Minister at 
a public function in recognition of performance.

nd February,2013 thus showing underutilisa tion of 66.71crores.  At B.E. 2013-14,

implementation of 6
th pay commission recommendations. There are also indications of

15.4 The Committee commends the measures taken by the Department to attract 
and retain Indian scientists who have se ttled in various parts of the world for 
pursuing research in India in their respectiv e field of expertise as well as in home 
country research programs and notes with satisfaction that measures taken have led 
to reversal of flow of researchers.  The Committee recommends that further 
measures be taken to make career in sc ience, research and innovation lucrative 
enough to attract best talent available in the country.   
16. NEW PROGRAMMES PLANNED DURING THE XII PLAN        
16.1 The Department of Science and Technology has started two major new 
programmes namely “Building National Capaci ty and Capability for High Performance 
Computing” and “National Geospatial Informat ion System” (NGIS) in the XII Five Year 
Plan. These are large nationally coordinate d projects with super-ordinate goals and 
expectations.  
16.2 These two programmes have been a llocated budgetary support amounting to 
.100.00 crores and .200.00 crores respec tively at B.E. 2013-14.  The Committee 
desired to know the aims and objectives of these new programmes and the roadmap 
drawn under National Geographic Informati on System (NGIS) to enable smooth 
transition of the country from e-governance to geo-spatial governance.  A brief account 
of aims and objectives of these two schemes provided by the Department is given below:-  
16.3 SUPER COMPUTING FACILITY AND CAPACITY BUILDING : 
The Planning Commission has drawn a Na tional Supercomputing Roadmap in the 
XII Plan which covers seve ral aspects of supercompu ting, namely, architecture, 
supercomputing grid resting on National Know ledge Network and the million core cloud 
supercomputer.  The aim of the scheme is  to undertake projected development of high 
capacity petascale (over 1,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputers and technologies 
that may create an opening lead ing to building Exa-scale (over 
1,000,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputing capability.  It also aims at capacity 
and capability development in the area of hardware and more in the area of application 
software to meet the demands of the scientif ic community from all disciplines. The DST, 
the Department of Electronics & Information Technology (Deity) in consultation with the 
Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru and Center for Development of Advance 
Computing (C-DAC), Pune, are preparin g the strategies for implementing the 
Programme. 
16.4  NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (NGIS) 
The NGIS has been set up with the objectives of establishing a “National GIS” as a 
Decision Support GIS-platform with a systematic nation-wide, seamless GIS Asset and to 
realise an organisational stru cture of Indian National GIS Organisation (INGO) that will 
be responsible for National GIS system, maintaining and operating the GIS Platform. 
16.5 The NGIS Mission will also organise the GSIS Asset-GIS database for the whole 
country for the first time.  The Mission woul d also develop National GIS Applications 
software suite required fo r different Ministries for governance. According to the 
Department, the Major elements of the Na tional GIS platform include creation of 

National GIS infrastructure, GIS portal development, National GIS standardization and 
process definition would be a key for success of National GIS.   
16.6 An innovative mission struct ure is planned for implem entation of National GIS, 
which would take care of overlaps and integration and alignment of all efforts to National 
GIS. The apex body of NGIS will be the National GIS Advisory Board (NAB) to provide 
overall policy-direction, advi ce/guide, and review to a ssess performance and suggest 
improvements and fine tuning of Mission and also function as the think tank for NGIS.  
16.7 DST has also constituted a High Power Governing Council (HPGC), with 
Secretaries of Department of Space, the Department of Electronics & Information 
Technology (Deity) and Ministry of Earth Scie nces as Co-Chairs.  A full time Mission 
Director would also be selected with a small and nimble NGIS Mission Directorate. 
16.8 The Committee feels that the above programmes are of great national 
importance and hence recommends that the Department should make every possible 
effort to successfu lly implement them in a time bound manner.  The Committee, 
further, recommends that the Department must ensure that the allocated outlays for 
these two schemes are fully utilized. 
17. The Committee hopes that Department of Science & Technology shall make 
prudent utilisation of funds allocated to it under Demand No. 85 for the year 2013-
14 having due regard to the recommendations made by the Committee and 
efficiently implement its various programmes and schemes in the year 2013-14.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTORY 
 Environment, over the years, has emerged as a key component a nd all pervading theme 
on the broader contours of economic growth w ithin sustainable development framework.  
Environmental concerns in the process of developmental philosophy have, however, 
sharpened further in the recent years with  the consequences of the environmental 
degradation manifesting in numerous ways su ch as global warming, scanty and scattered 
rainfall, changing weather pattern, depleting glaciers, receding water flow in major rivers, 
poor and pathetic state of e nvironmental resources – land, ai r & water and their adverse 
impact on human health, etc. also known as climate cha nge on the one hand and with 
blatant, brazen and reckless exploitation of natural reso urces resulting in massive 
deforestation and degeneration of green covers on the other.  As recently as on 18th April, 
2013, Supreme Court, in its landmark judgment,  decreed that environment & ecology are 
national assets, they are subject to interg enerational equity a nd the principle of 
sustainable development has been  rendered as part of Articl e 21 of the Constitution of 
India.  Yet, the national commitment to a clean and healthy environment as enshrined in 
Articles 48(a) and 51(a)(g) of the Indian Constitution and the aspiration that human 
beings should be able to enj oy a decent quality of  life remains a far cry.  The reasons are 
not far too difficult to find out.  The fact is that the reas ons are both obvious and opaque.  
An evolving and expanding society, such as  ours, in desperate pursuit of economic 
prosperity for poverty alleviation, livelihood secu rity and restoration of  greater justice to 
those deprived is bound to c onfront environmental challe nges.  Secondly, exponential 
population growth, inappropriate  technology, consumption choi ces, paradigm shift in 
amicable and harmonious relationship of co-existence between people and ecosystem, 
proliferation of polluting indus tries, unplanned urbanisation, etc. have prominently and 

routinely been attributed to be the chie f drivers of environmental degradation and 
ecological imbalances.  But there are certain ot her latent yet potent contributory factors 
which need attention and focus too.  These ar e institutional failures resulting in lack of 
enforcement of rights of access to and use of  environmental resources, failed and flawed 
regulatory regime, governance constrains in environmental management, policy lacunae, 
disincentivising  environmen tal conservation, to mention a few.  The widely 
acknowledged fact that not much could be done to manage the former category of 
prominent factors catapults us to concentrate more on the latter ones as to how best we 
can overcome them.  Sooner or later, this ha s to be done in recogni tion of the axiomatic 
fact that environmental resources play pivot al role not only in pr oviding livelihoods but 
also in securing life supportin g ecological services to all forms of life – human, animal 
and plant.  But, the sooner done is better because environmental damages beyond a 
certain degree, become irreparable and irreversible.   
2. It, therefore, becomes imperative for al l of us to gear and galvanize all the 
resources at our disposal to minimize if not  altogether eliminate the possibilities of 
collateral damage done to the environment, ecology, forests and wildlife. 
3.  Environment is universal, ubiquitous and all pervasiv e comprising of entities – 
natural or manmade, external to oneself and their interrelationships, which provide value 
now or perhaps in the future to mankind.  Mana ging such a vast and wi der rather infinite 
spectrum of challenges, is undoubtedly a daun ting task entrusted to  the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests as a nodal agency in the administrative setup of the Govt. of 
India.  The ministry, since its inception on 4
th January, 1985 has been, through thick and 
thins of overriding and pres sing priorities, sometimes c onflicting and contradictory 
engaged in trying to strike a fine bala nce by planning, promoting, coordinating and 
overseeing environmental, ecological forestry and wildlife programmes and policies.  The 
main activities of the Ministry involve prot ection of the environment; conservation and 
survey of existing forests, wildlife, aqua tic bodies, water resources and eco-systems 
including biodiversity and ot her resources particularly in eco-sensitive zones for 
identification of new species of flora and fauna; afforestation and regeneration of 
degraded areas; prevention and control of pollution (air, water, noise, industrial); 
management of hazardous substances; mitigation and adaptation to climate change 
through adoption of cleaner technologies; pr omotion of sustainable development and 
better environmental governance; ensuring welfare of animals; capacity building; training 
and research in classical and molecular taxonomy; etc.  Apart from these national 
activities, the Ministry is also engaged in promoting in ternational cooperation through 
regional, bilateral and multilateral initiatives in the arena of environment and ecology.  
Issues relating to regional bodies like Economic and Social  Council for Asia & Pacific 
(ESCAP) and South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) and 
multilateral bodies such as the Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD); Global 
Environment Facility (GEF) have been entruste d to the Ministry.  Besides, the Ministry 
also serves as the nodal agency for the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), 
South Asia Cooperation Environment Programme  (SACEP) and Intern ational Centre for 
Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMD) , as well as, for follow up on the United 
Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED).  
4. Institutional Setup
 
4.1 The Institutional setup of the Minist ry includes a number of Directorates, 
Divisions, Regional Offices, Subordinate Offi ces, Boards, Autonomous Institutions and 
one Public Sector Undertaking, the details of which are as follows:- 

 
(a) Regional Offices: -  The Ministry has six Regional Offices covering 
various Zones of the country.  The No rth Zone Regional Office is located 
at Chandigarh; the Central Zone at Lucknow; the Northeastern Zone at 
Shillong and Bhubaneswar; the South Zone at Bengaluru; the Eastern 
plateau or upper East at Ranchi and the West Zone at Bhopal.   
(b) Subordinate Offices: -
  
(i) Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata;  
(ii) Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata;  
(iii) National Museum of Natural History, New Delhi;

(v) Directorate of Forest Education, Dehradun;  
(vi) Forest Survey of India Dehradun;  
(vii) National Zoological Park, New Delhi; and  
(viii) National Institute of Animal Welfare, Faridabad. 
(c) Aided Autonomous Institutions/ Statutory Bodies/ Registered 
Societies: - (i)  Environment and Ecology  
 Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Delhi; 
 G.B. Pant Institute of Himalayan Environment &
