20.6.3 Even the Planning Commission’s 12
th Five Year Plan Approach Paper states that 
as the Indian economy and society grow and modernize, the Indian Science and 
Technology landscape also has to change to meet the magnitude of new demands being 
made.  The paper also stresses the need fo r creating a strong R &D system within the 
scientific sector.  According to it, at pres ent, R& D expenditure in the country is only 
0.9% of GDP, of which about 3/4 th is in the public sector and only 1/4 th in the private 
sector.  This R &D expenditure at 0.9% of  GDP is, however, not at all adequate to 
develop strong R & D base needed as principle driving force for economic growth.  
20.6.4 The Committee notes with concern that  India is lagging far behind other 
countries of the world in respect of R & D contribution made by the Private sector.  
In comparison to developed countries of the world, India’s R&D funding from non-
government sector is abysmally low.  Ev en in comparison to our neighboring 
country China, we lag far behind. The percentage contribution of private sector and 
public sector to R&D contribut ion in India & China is nearly in reverse order.  In 
China private sector contribution is near ly 70% of R&D expenditure while in India 
it is Government which makes 75 to 80% co ntribution.  The Committee feels that in 
order to enhance funding in R&D, the private R&D contribution needs to be 
augmented substantially.  The Committee in its 227 th report had recommended that 
private sector contribution to   R&D needs to be enhanced to 50% from 25% during 

the 12 th Plan period by offering incentive s, forming partnership etc.  The 
Department in their Action Taken Rep lies had assured the Committee that every 
effort would be made to bring industries on board. Even the Government has in 
their 12th Five Year Plan Approach Paper admitt ed that private sector contribution 
is not adequate to develop strong R &D .  The Committee feels that somewhere we 
have failed in our efforts to woo private sector and nothing commendable has been 
achieved in this direction even in th e second year of the plan period.  The 
Committee, therefore, feels that mere assura nce given by the Department to make 
every effort to bring Industries on board,  will not help unless it draws a concrete 
time bound action plan to ensure that pr ivate sector contribution to R&D gets 
enhanced to 50% from existing 25% by the end of 12
th Five Year Plan.  
20.7 New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) 
20.7.1 The Department has informed that  New Millennium Indian Technology 
Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) is a landmar k Public Private Partnership R&D scheme 
aimed at delivering cutting edge technologies  to provide India a global leadership 
position in select niche areas. During XI Five Year Plan, NMITLI has provided a unique 
platform for performing R&D in public-private partnership (PPP) mode.  
20.7.2 So far, NMITLI has evolve d 75 largely networked proj ects in diverse areas viz. 
Agriculture & Plant Biotechnology, General Biotechnology, Bioinformatics, Drugs & 
Pharmaceuticals, Chemicals, Materials, Information and Communication Technology and 
Energy. These projects involve  100 industry partners & 300 R&D groups from different 
institutions.  
20.7.3 During the XII Plan period, NMITLI pr ogramme will continue with its main 
objective and develop innovation based technologies. The programme looks beyond 
today’s technology and thus seeks to build, cap ture and retain for India a leadership 
position by synergizing the best competen cies of publicly funded R&D institutions, 
academia and private industry. The strategy adop ted for NMITLI is to obtain an inverse 
risk investment profile, i.e., low investme nt in high-risk technology areas (with global 
leadership potential) with investments increasing as developments take place and the 
projects move up on the innovation curve with reduction in risks.  
20.7.4 The NMITLI programme was allocated Rs. 60 crores at B.E. 2012-13 which was 
reduced to Rs. 40.00 crores at R.E. 2012-13 an d Rs. 45.00 crores has b een kept at B.E. 
2013-14 for this programme.   
20.7.5 The Committee in its 227
th report had recommended the following: 
 “The Committee feels that in view of budgetary constraints, there is a need for the 
Department to devise innovative ways for funding these schemes.  Public Private 
Partnership (PPP) model, levy of appropriate user charges, funding from other 
beneficiaries, sharing of profits arising fr om commercial exploitation of patents funded 
under schemes, etc. are some of the known ways in which requisite funds for 
implementation of schemes can be generate d.  The Committee hopes that the Department 
would be able to devise innov ative ways of funding schemes & achieve the targets set for 
2012-13 under these schemes.  The Committee, however, feels that Government should, 
to the extent necessary, provide adequate funds for these schemes at RE stage, so that 
targets set for 2012-13 under these schemes get realised in toto”.  
20.7.6 The Department in their reply had stated the following: 
 “The Department is in the process of obtaining the necessary approvals for the 
schemes and shall be able to mobilise the necessary funding for the same”. 

20.7.7 The Department informed the Committee that CSIR was monitoring projects 
under NMITLI Scheme very rigorously through Steering Committee after every 3 months 
and through Monitoring Committee after ever y 6 months. These committees review and 
ensure that projects are implemented as per plan. Financial progress is monitored through 
Utilization Certificates obtained twice a year. Funds are rel eased based on the Utilization 
Certificates. CSIR will continue these step s in the year 2013-14 also. CSIR is also 
sensitizing about risk coverage in PPP mode of R&D. 
20.7.8 The Committee appreciates that New Millennium I ndian Technology 
Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) star ted by the Department in the 11
th Plan and 
recommends that programme should be pursued with great vigour in the 12 th Plan 
so that a large number of research projects are undertaken under PPP mode and 
private investment in R&D which, at present is around 20 to 25%, increase 
substantially. 
20.8 CSIR 800  
20.8.1 During the 12 th Five Year Plan Period, CSIR has initiated a new full-fledged 
scheme ‘CSIR-800’ with the broad objective to  augment the incomes and the quality of 
the lives of one million rural citizens geogr aphically spread across the country, in 
accordance with stated Government of India targets and relevant UN-Millennium 
Development Goals. The strategic implementation of the scheme focuses on building and 
operating ‘CSIR Technology-enabled Villages’ (TECHVIL) at twenty -five to thirty 
locations, where the proportion of families living in poverty is high. Each TECHVIL 
would cater to about 40,000 people and act as  a source of relevant technological 
interventions and skill development for them.  
20.8.2. The Committee enquired about the crite ria for choosing a TECHVIL. In their 
reply, the Department has informed that CSIR-800 scheme has identified the districts that 
were declared backward by the Planning Commission in 2001 and 2010 and also figure in 
the list identified for joint action w ith the UN under UNDAF (UN Development 
Assistance Framework); RGF (Rajiv Gandhi  Foundation); and/or PACS (Poorest Areas 
Civil Society). CSIR labs are under proces s of finalizing the locations for several 
TECHVILs in consultation with concerned st ate agencies, local communities and other 
stakeholders. Further, CSIR along with AcSI R has identified domain expert scientists, 
students and academics for implementation of the CSIR-800 scheme. 
20.8.3 The Committee lauds the objective with which CSIR 800 scheme has been 
launched.  The fact that more budgetary allocation has been made for the scheme 
than those demanded by the Department shows the importance that Government 
attaches to this scheme.  The Committee hopes that the Department shall endeavour 
to achieve the objective of the scheme of augmenting the income and quality of lives 
of one million rural citizens across the country during the 12
th Five Year Plan.  The 
Committee also recommends that the Depa rtment should formulate more such 
schemes to augment the income of poor and quality of their lives. 
20.9 CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation  
20.9.1 The Committee desired to know the detail s of CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation, 
Initiative for Inclusive, Participative and Collaborative Research & Development. The 
Department informed that in order to ma ke healthcare affordable to the common man, 
Open Source Drug Discovery programme (O SDD) was initiated by the Department 
during the 11th Five Year Plan. It was, furt her believed that the current Intellectual 
Property based models of pharmaceutical innov ation do not address the diseases of the 
poor such as Tuberculosis. The OSDD progra mme has now emerged as a new platform 

for innovation in the domain of healthcare particularly for treating diseases like 
Tuberculosis, Malaria, etc.  
20.9.2 CSIR is consolidating and taking forw ard the gains of OSDD to the 12th Five 
Year Plan. OSDD started with TB as the target disease but during the 12
th Five Year Plan 
it proposes to expand its drug discovery activities  to Malaria and Leishmaniasis       
(Kala-Azar) and launch clinical trials of a TB drug. The affordable healthcare principle 
underlies all activities of OSDD and would c over (a) Open Source Drug Discovery; (b) 
Open Source Drug Development; (c) Open Source Drug Delivery; and (d) Open Source 
Disease Diagnostics. CSIR further informed the Committee that for the financial year 
2013-14, the Department has projected Rs. 109 cr ores out of which only Rs. 70 crore has 
been approved. 
20.9.3 The Committee desired to know the time fr ame within which it would target to 
complete its clinical trials for diseases like TB, Malaria, Kala-Azar etc.  The Department 
informed that they were in the process of f iling an application for permission to initiate 
clinical trials before the Directorate of Controller Ge neral of India (DCGI). Upon 
approval, the trial would be initiated in co llaboration with LRS Hospital for Respiratory 
and Infectious Diseases, New Delhi, a hospita l under Ministry of Health. This provides a 
novel model where publicly funded institutes are contributing together to bring drugs for 
treatment of diseases of poor like TB.  
20.9.4 Further the Department has also stated that Drug discovery and development is a 
long and risky endeavour plagued with uncertainti es. It will not be appropriate to provide 
a completion date to clinical trials. CSIR may initiate a clinical trial for Malaria, if an 
appropriate drug candidate is available, during the plan period. 
20.9.5 The Committee appreciates the novel objective of its Open Source Drug 
Discovery Plan i.e. to make healthcare affordable to the common man.  The 
Committee notes that the programme was initiated in 11
th Five Year Plan with TB 
as target disease and is being extended to 12 th Five Year Plan to cover Malaria and 
Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar) and hopes that  programme would lead to affordable 
treatment of these diseases for common man.  The Committee recommends that the 
Department should provide high priority to such socially useful programmes so that 
objectives of these programmes are achieved as early as possible.  
20.10 National Civil Aircraft De velopment Programme (NCAD)  
20.10.1    The Department of Scientific and Indu strial Research is known for its research 
and innovative ideas. In its que st for expanding its research  activities in  the aviation 
sector on one hand and break th e shackles of dependence on import of civil aircrafts on 
the other, CSIR muster courage and initia ted an over ambitious venture termed as 
National Civil Aircraft Programme (NCAD).  NCAD will be a 90 seater civil aircraft to 
be built with state of the art techniques de veloped with CSIR-NAL collaboration. It is 
included in the 12
th Five Year Plan of CSIR as a New Scheme.  
20.10.2    For the current financial year (2013- 14), an allocation of Rs. 10 crore has been 
made, as against the projected demand of Rs. 178 crores. 
20.10.3   The Committee in its 227
th Report had recommended the following: 
“The Committee hopes that formal Government approval for the programme 
would be available soon and the programme woul d start in right earnes t at the earliest.  
The Committee is also of the view that this  programme is of great national importance 
and sufficient funds be made av ailable to this programme so that our own indigenous 90 
seater aircraft becomes a reality in a short time from now”.  

20.10.4   The Committee enquired about the pr ogress made under this programme since 
last year. While informing the Committee about  the progress made so far, CSIR stated 
about the constitution of two Committees i.e.  Committee for creating Joint Venture (JV) 
for NCAD and a Technical Committee. The Te rm of Reference (TOR) of JV Committee 
was to: (i) identify industry partner (s) through a transparent exercise and work out the 
modalities for the JV formulation, (ii) suggest  equity structure of the identified industry 
partner(s), and (iii) give necessary inputs to CSIR for developing a cabinet note for 
obtaining in-principle approval for the implementation of the programme as 
recommended by the Planning Commission. The JV Committee interacted with a number 
of Indian business houses to develop an Expr ession of Interest (EO I) and a draft Cabinet 
note. The JV interim report has been fina lized. The Technical Committee would guide 
the programme, identify work modules and wo uld also provide inputs for developing a 
Cabinet Note for obtaining ‘in-principle’ a pproval. Based on the recommendations of the 
two Committees, the National Civil Aircraft  Development Programme  would be finally 
formulated.  
20.10.5       Further, CSIR-NAL has made an assessment of the programme by carrying 
out a Feasibility Study for the development of a 70-90 seat er National Civil Aircraft. The 
Feasibility Study Report included Market  Assessment, Configuration Definition, 
Development Strategy, Cost Estimates and th e Business Model. As per the Feasibility 
study, the total estimated cost of the project  is Rs 7555 crore out of which Rs 4355 crore 
is for design & development phase and Rs 3200 crore for series production phase of the 
aircraft. Both the phases would involve Joint Venture with private sector. 
20.10.6    The Committee is perturbed to obs erve that very little progress has been 
made with regard to this important programme. In order to develop capabilities for 
development of aircrafts with large passenger capacities, the Committee is of the 
view that the Department should complete this programme at the earliest so that 
new programme of development of more so phisticated aircrafts of even higher 
passenger capacities could be taken and India acquires capabilities to compete with 
established countries like USA and France in  this field.  The Committee accordingly 
recommends that the Department should se riously work for successful completion 
of the programme at the earliest.  
20.11   Programme for North-Eastern States and Women centric initiatives 
20.11.1   Like any Department of the Government  of India, DSIR also enunciates various 
programmes/schemes for the North-Eastern States and Women centric programmes like 
Technology Development and Utiliza tion program for Women and Women 
Entrepreneurship Development programme.  In order to improve productivity, 
employment, livelihood especially for the backward women, unemployed youths and for 
facilitating new avenues of employment genera tion and income generating activities, for 
which the Department has earmarked the task to one of its public sector enterprises i.e 
NRDC.  According to the Annual Report of the Department, NRDC organized various 
programme for the people of North Eastern States like skill development training 
programme on handloom weaving for unempl oyed youth, development of high land 
water harvesting for drinking and piscicul ture-cum-irrigation reservoir, skilled 
development programme on computer traini ng, food/fruit processing for unemployed 
youths and women’s empowerment programme on kauna crafts.   
20.11.2   Further, Women Entrepreneurship Development Programme (WEDP) aimed at 
promoting, inspiring and encouraging women st udents at different le vels from various 
universities/colleges to take up entrepreneurship to empower themselves. Besides, NRDC 

also conducted skill development progr ams for women like program in bakery 
production, fruits and vegetable processing etc.  
20.11.3   The Committee notes skill development training programme organized by 
NRDC for the people of North Eastern St ates & for women’s empowerment and is 
particularly happy on setting up of post harvest technology centres.  The Committee 
recommends that in order to assess the potency and utility of these training 
programmes, the Department should develo p a mechanism to find out as to what 
extent these training progr ammes have actua lly resulted in trained persons 
becoming gainfully employed or becoming entrepreneurs because that alone will 
demonstrate the usefulness of these programmes. 
20.12   PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES  
20.12.1   National Research Development Corporation (NRDC)   
20.12.2    National Research Development Co rporation (NRDC) was incorporated on 
31st December, 1953 as a Section 25 comp any under the Companies Act with an 
objective to promote, develop and commercia lize indigenous technologies. As per the 
objectives set out in its Me morandum and Articles of Asso ciation, NRDC was mandated 
to commercialize the technologies devel oped by all the resear ch laboratories and 
institutes of CSIR and other public funded re search institutes, un iversities including 
autonomous research institutions.  
20.12.3 The Committee enquired from the Depart ment about the efforts made by the 
NRDC to promote, develop and commercia lize indigenous technologies as per its 
mandate and the profit earned through that promotions/developments/commercialization 
of indigenous technologies.  The Department in their repl y has informed that National 
Research Development Corporation (NRDC) is engaged in obtaining assignment of 
technologies from various research institut ions and universities in the country for 
commercialization. During the last three years,  a total of 141 technologies and technical 
know-hows were assigned to the Corporati on by various R&D institutions across the 
country for commercialization. NRDC assists the technology developers i.e. research 
institutions / universities in  patenting their inventions, technologies and technical know-
hows, if they so desire. Out of the 141 t echnologies and technical know-hows assigned to 
NRDC during the last three years, 22 have been filed for patent protection by the research 
institutions / universities themselves. NR DC provided assistance for filing patent 
applications for 37 technologies and the rema ining were without patent protection. The 
total revenue generated by NRDC  in terms of lump-sum premium and royalty by way of 
licensing, marketing and commercialization of th e said technologies during the last three 
years is Rs.1968 lakhs.  
20.12.4   However, according to the Annual Report, for the year 2011-12, the 
Corporation incurred loss to the tune of Rs. 84.54 Lakhs (befor e tax) as compared to loss 
of Rs. 158.23 Lakhs in the previous year. The Committee notes with concern the poor 
performance of NRDC. The Committee feel s that the purpose for which an 
organization is created gets defeated if it fails to deliver.  The mandate of NRDC is 
to commercialize the technologies developed by the research laboratories and 
institutes of CSIR and other public funded research institutes, universities including 
autonomous research institutions. The p oor record of NRDC in obtaining patents 
for technologies & technical knowhow assigned to it, coupled with losses incurred by 
it, speaks volumes of its malfunctioning & lack of professionalism.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should introspect the causes of failure 

of NRDC and its poor performance and work  out a strategy to ensure that NRDC is 
in a position to fulfill the purpose for which it was established.  
20.13  Central Electronics Limited (CEL)  
20.13.1  CEL’s operations can be broadly grouped into three areas, viz. solar 
photovoltaics (SPV), strategic electronics and railway electronics. CEL is the pioneer and 
a leading manufacturer of SPV cells, modules  and systems and Railway Safety Signaling 
Equipment. In the field of st rategic electronics, CEL is th e only indigenous manufacturer 
of phase control modules, which is a key element of phased array radars.  
20.13 .2   The Committee in its 227th Report had recommended the following: 
“Planning Commission must ensure that crucial programmes like up gradations 
of photovoltaic module are not starved of funds and adequate allocations be made to 
these programmes at the RE stage”.   
20.13.3  CEL has been allocated Rs 8 crore dur ing 2013-14, whereas it has estimated an 
outlay of Rs 15 crores for the project on en hancing the capacity of solar PV module 
production facility from 10 MW to 25 MW. CEL has informed that they would like to 
seek additional funds for the project at the RE  stage 2013-14 or else it will continue and 
complete the project during 2014-15.  
20.13.4  CEL has informed that for enhancing the capacity of sola r photovoltaic (PV) 
module production from 10 MW to 80 MW fund re quirement has been worked out to Rs 
80 Crore. However, due to budget constrai nts, the project has been modified as 
“Development & Up-gradation of PV Modul e Manufacturing Facility” by reducing the 
anticipated up-graded capaci ty of PV module production to 25 MW. CEL has estimated 
that it would require 10 months for the installation and commissioning of all the 
equipments to upgrade the capacity of solar photovoltaic module production facility from 
10 MW to 25 MW, provided it is made available the requisite funds.  
20.13.5  The Committee enquired from the Department about the allocation of funds/ 
profit earned by CEL for upgrading photovolta ic modules and the performance of CEL 
over the years. In response thereto, the De partment has stated that CEL has incurred 
persistent losses. The performance of CEL during the last three years is given below:

20.13.6   The Committee notes with concern losses being incurred by CEL in the 
years 2010-11 & 2011-12 and recommends that Department should take necessary 
measures to restore its financial viabil ity.  The Committee fu rther express its 
anguish that due to financial crunch the crucial programme of upgradation of the 
capacity of solar photo volta ic module from 10 MW to 80 MW is held up and funds 
made available are not even sufficient to upg rade the production facility to 25 MW 
in this financial year and unless sufficient funds are made available even 
upgradation of the production facility to 25 MW would be possible only in 2014-15.  
The Committee recommends that fund crunch should not hold up upgradation of 
facilities for production of photo voltaic module and sufficient funds be allocated at

 REPORT 
The long history of Biotechnology had w itnessed productive use of biological 
processes to create useful goods for th e benefit of mankind. Rapid scientific 
developments in the past few decades have produced a knowledge base and set of tools 
and techniques that enable biological pro cesses to be better unders tood and controlled to 
an extent never possible before. During th e first half of the 20th century, knowledge 
from the scientific fields of Chemistry and Genetics, combined to provide a revolution in 
the field of life sciences. Advances in ge netic engineering since 1953 had led to the 
acceptance of the role of DNA, combined with its molecular structure, to bring about the 
development of new tools and techniques in genetic engineering, which in turn brought 
about huge advances in biotechnology. As of today biotechnology is applicable in 
diverse fields like healthcare, food, mining, plastics, agriculture and animal husbandry 
etc.   
1.1 With a view to give a new impetus to the development in the field of modern 
biology and biotechnology, as mentioned abov e, in the country, the Government of 
India, initially set up an  Independent Board in 1982, which became a full-fledged 
Department of Biotechnology under Minist ry of Science & Technology in 1986.  The 
Department of Biotechnology is today a ma jor national research and development 
agency and provides nearly two-third of the Research & Development support in the life 
science sector in the country. The Depa rtment endeavours to wards creating an 
institutional framework and human resour ces for nurturing scie nce and technology for 
advancement in their respective fields. To nur ture ever augmenting growth in the field 
of Biotechnology, the budgetary allocation of the Department has been increased from 
around Rs.23.00 crores in 1986-87 to over Rs . 1500.00 crores in 2013-14. The Indian 
biotech industry had expande d threefold during 2009-11 to record revenues of US $3 
billion and is expected to grow further in the coming years.  
2. MANDATE  OF THE DEPARTMENT 
2.1 The main mandate of the Depart ment of Biotechnology is as under:- 
 To evolve policies and integrated progr ammes in biotechnology and ensure their 
implementation and monitoring;  

 To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and 
manufacturing in biologicals and biot echnology and oversee the initiation and 
pursuit of related research and manufacturing activities;  
 To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and 
Development in biotechnology and ensure pr oper dovetailing of their activities as 
per national priorities and objectives;  
 To act as a screening, advising and appr oving agent of the Government with 
regard to import and transfer of ne w technologies for the manufacture of 
biologicals, biotechnological products and their intermediates;  
 Evolve safety guidelines for biotec hnology Research and Development and 
manufacturing in India;  
 To act as the central agency for the impor t of genetically manipulated materials, 
culture, cells, specimens, tissues and biotech produc ts including DNA and RNA 
of any type or size and for promoting their production in the country;  
 Serve as the inter-ministerial and in teragency nodal point for all specific 
international bilateral and multilateral Research and Development collaborations 
and agreements in the area of biotec hnology and act as the nodal point for all 
technology transfers in the area of biotechnology;  
 Manufacture and ensure application of  recombinant, cell-based and DNA 
vaccines, diagnostics and other biotechnological products;  
 To evolve programmes for Human Res ource Development in the area of 
biotechnology;  
 Serve as an administrative and impl ementing Department of agencies, 
commissions, boards, etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the 
national objectives in biotechnology and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-
informatics including training and cr eation of infrastr ucture, collection, 
dissemination and exchange of information relating to biotechnology; 
 Establishment of National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority;   
 To deal with matters relating to the following institutions:

back i.e. in 2003 and the current level of investment is only 0.9% of GDP. The 
Department explained that the 12
th Plan document of Science & Technology published by 
Planning Commission, states that “to achieve the target of gr oss R&D expenditure of 2% 
of GDP additional Government efforts as also  much increased private sector effort is

would pursue such programmes for contributi on towards increasing R&D expenditure in 
S&T to reach to about 2% targeted by the end of 12th Plan.  
6.4 The Committee further notes that as  per new Science, Technology & Innovation 
Policy(STI), 2013, while Global investments in science, technology and innovation are 
estimated at $1.2 trillion as of 2009. India’s R&D investment is less than 2.5% of this 
amount and is currently under 1% of the GDP.  Increasing Gross Expenditure in Research 
and Development (GERD) to 2% of the GDP has been a national goal for some time and 
achieving this in the next five years is real izable if the private sector raises its R&D 
investment to at least match the public sector  R&D investment from the current ratio of 
around 1:3 and this seems attainable as the industrial R&D investment grew by 250% and 
the sales by 200% between 2005 and 2010.  Increa sed private investment is necessary for 
translating R&D outputs into commercial outco mes. While maintaining current rates of 
growth in public R&D investments, a cond ucive environment will be created for 
enhancing private sector investment in R&D. 
6.5 The Committee notes with concern low le vel of private sector investment in 
R&D and is of the view that Department should effectively leverage its Public 
Private Partnership Programme to catalyze increasing private sector investment in 
R&D in Biotechnology.  The Committee no tes with appreciation that through 
Biotechnology Industry Partnership Progra mme of the Department, 85 companies 
are already investing in 102 projects a nd recommends that the Department of 
Biotechnology should pursue such program mes, which would build a conducive 
environment for increased private sector investment in R&D in Biotechnology, so 
that the national goal of increasing expe nditure in Research and Development in 
S&T to 2% of GDP in next five years is realised.  The Committee is of the firm 
opinion that national aspiration of posi tioning India among the top five global 
scientific powers by 2020 can only be realised by significantly augmenting 
investments in R&D in S&T and accordin gly, the Committee recommends that the 
Planning Commission must provide sufficie nt funds to the R&D programme of the 
Department to meet this national objective.   

7. INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FO R GENETIC ENGINEERING AND 
BIOTECHNOLOGY(ICGEB) 
7.1 The Department informed that the IC GEB acts as a centre of excellence for 
research and training in genetic engineering & biotechnology and also meets the needs of 
the developing world to function as a formal international mechanism and forum to 
channelise and coordinate sc ientific and technological reso urces available in developed 
countries in the area of genetic engineeri ng and biotechnology. It was further informed 
that, the ICGEB is an international organisa tion of 65 member c ountries and has been 
established as a two component centre, with a centre at Trieste, Italy and the other at New 
Delhi by United Nations International Develo pment Organization and has been granted 
an independent status from February 1994 afte r its statute came into  force. The main 
thrust of the centre has been to carry out ba sic research in the areas of human diseases 
and agriculture focusing mainly on research relevant to the Indian subcontinent.  
7.2 Informing the Committee of the proposed activities of th e Centre for the year                 
2013-14, the Department informed that programmes like Malaria Vaccine  development, 
research on Hepatitis C virus, Dengue  Vaccine, Translational programme for 
development of transgenic rice, onion, toma to etc, and Lab space expansion, which were 
earlier being handled by the Centre would continue during the year 2013-14.  
7.3 During the examination of Demands  for Grants(2012-13), the Committee 
analysed in detail the status and functi oning of the ICGEB and found that it was 
functioning on the basis of the financial grants  received from the Government of Italy for 
the last 6 years, which had remained more or less static with contribution marginally 
reduced during financial year  2011-12. The Co mmittee further noted that the Centre was 
receiving a Non Plan allocation of Rs 10.00 cror es from the Government of India, which 
was discontinued from the year 2012-13. While examining all these issues, the 
Committee formed a view in its 228
th Report, that the research centres engaged in applied 
science should not be supporte d on Government funds for a long period and the Institute 
must develop its capability to raise resources by  commercially exploiting its product and 
services. The Committee formed such opinion on the basis of the fact that when Italian 
Government had reduced its grant for r unning the centre in 2012-13 and also the 
Government of India discontinued its Non Plan allocation made earlier for the centre. The 
Committee feared that the cumulative effect of these cuts, may lead to financial crisis for 
the centre to run, consequently adversely affecting its functioning and ongoing research 
programmes. The Committee as a measure to come out from such impending crisis, 
recommended in its aforesaid report that inte rim financial assistance  be provided to the 
centre to tide over its immediate problem and al so advocated that the centre should make 
effort to meet its expenses from its own income, in order to avoid its dependence on 
government and foreign funds. 
7.4 In the 238
th Action Taken Report of the Committee, the Department while  
recognising the significance of the aforesaid observation, me ntioned that it had held 
elaborate discussions with ICGEB governi ng body for developing strategy to address 
financial sustainability of the Centre on a long term-basis. The Department further 
informed that during the 12 th Plan, a special budget head  i.e. ‘Autonomous R& D 
Institutions’ had been introduced and a pr ovision of  Rs. 13.00 crores had been made 
under the said head for the centre for the year 2012-13, out of which Rs. 650 lakhs had 
been released to ICGEB. 
7.5 In pursuance of the above decision of  the Government, arising out of the 
recommendations of the Committee, no separa te budgetary allocation had been made for 

ICGEB for B.E. 2013-14 and instead the allocation for ICGEB has been shown under the 
head ‘Autonomous R& D Institutions’ and as already mentioned above and a token 
amount of Rs. 13.00 crores had been allocated to  the said centre.  The Department also 
informed that as part of the future plans, it had already constituted a high-level 
Committee to examine the matters related to  operation of the ICGEB, which would 
recommend the possible restructured model for the sustainability of the institution on a 
long-term basis, in view of the decreased fi nancial support from Italian Government and 
stoppage of non plan allocation by the gove rnment. The first meeting of the said 
Committee was held on 9
th March, 2013 at Bangalore.    
7.6 The Committee is happy to note that in response to its recommendation 
contained in 228th Report, the Department  has as a part of its efforts to address the 
issue of financial sustainability of the cen tre, constituted a high-level Committee to 
examine the matters related to operati on of the ICGEB and the high level 
Committee would inter-alia recommend the possible restructured model for the 
sustainability of the institution on a long-term basis.  The Committee notes that the 
main thrust of the centre is to carry out basic research in the areas of human 
diseases and agriculture focussing mainly on research relevant to the Indian sub-
continent and considering the importance of work entrusted to the centre, the 
Committee is keen that the centre func tions on a self sustained basis and 
accordingly, recommends that the Departme nt should ensure that the restructured 
model of the centre makes it financially viable on self sustainable basis.     
8. DEVELOPMENT OF BIOENERGY AND BIOFUELS 
8.1 The Bioenergy initiative of the Departme nt is to strengthen and expedite the 
bioenergy research and technology development in India. A strategic decision was made 
to set-up Bioenergy Centres at  three locations of India vi z. (i) DBT-ICT Centre for 
Energy Biosciences (Mumbai) was setup in the year 2008 to develop technology for 
second generation biofuel; (ii) DBT-IOC Ce ntre for Advanced Bioenergy Research 
(Faridabad) was setup to develop and de ploy second and third generation biofuel 
technologies with its existing capabilities to scale up; and (iii) DBT-ICGEB Centre for 
Advanced Bioenergy Research (New Delhi) was the third Centre setup in March 2012 to 
perform cutting-edge research using synthetic and system biology approaches towards the 
development of novel technology for biofuel production.  
8.2 The Committee was also informed of  the ‘The Bioenergy Road Map-Vision 
2020’, which had been prepared through a cons ultative process by an expert group of 
scientists involving all researchers from institu tes, universities and industries working in 
this area across the country.  
The Committee was informed of its goals and targets, which are as follows: 
 20% blending of fossil fuel by 2020; 
 Commercially viable lignoce llulosic ethanol produced from 
Agricultural and forestry waste;  
 An economically cost efficient system available for Algal 
production and also a commercial scale technology for production 
of biofuels from Algae eith er through harvesting and oil 
transesterification or direct conversion to Bio-oil; and  
 Next generation biofuels from different biomass feedstock.  
The Committee was also informed that presently, no commercially feasible 
second generation biofuel technologies are available in the country and this national need 
demands a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive technologies.  

8.3  In bioenergy area, major focus was to develop technolo gy for production of 
biofuels from agricultural wastes thr ough DBT sponsored collaborative centres and 
projects. The ICGEB Centre for Advanced  Bioenergy Research was successful in 
identification of three novel ce llulolytic enzymes, which are currently being tested in 
collaboration with Institute of Chemi cal Technology, Mumbai and Indian Oil 
Corporation Ltd.(IOCL), Faridabad. Inform ing the Committee of the new programmes, 
the Department stated that   a virtual Pan -IIT Centre for Bioenergy had been established 
and a joint proposal has been received from 5 IITs which is under review for further 
consideration. 
8.4 The issue of Bioenergy in the form of  ‘Jatropha Bio-diesel Mission Network 
Programme’ of the Department figured in th e discussion, relating to the Department’s 
meeting held on the 3
rd April, 2013, wherein the Committee was informed that at the 
beginning, Jatropha plant, a source of biofuel, was initially cultivated as a wild crop and 
the seeds were not of good quality. However, under the said Mission the Department in 
collaboration with the Ministry of New and Renewable Resources identified good quality 
Jatropha plant across  20 locations in 23 stat es in the country. Apart from this about 
15,000 plant excision were also collected for multi-location trials.  
8.5  As regards the issue of Bio-Etha nol, another bio-fuel, the Committee was 
informed that good quality material is already available at nine nurseries in Uttar Pradesh 
and the Lucknow Biotech Park had been made  the nodal agency for it. Besides, the 
Bharat Petroleum Company Limited, which is a Public Sector Company, had started its 
own plantation/nurseries for supply of good quality planting material. The Committee 
was also informed that the Bio-ethanol t echnology had been solely developed by the 
Department in collaboration with the Institute of Chemical Technology, Mumbai. 
Presently the technology is being perfect ed through the pilot plant set up at 
Kashipur(U.P.) and it was hoped that the te chnology would be available by the year end 
i.e December, 2013 for use on a commercial scale. Thereafter, the technology would be 
given to various user-agencies such as suga r mills, distillery units etc. for using this 
technology for commercial use. 
8.6 The Committee is aware of the pressing  need for finding non-conventional 
sources of clean energy and is happy to know  that Department in collaboration with 
the Institute of Chemical Technology, Mu mbai had succeeded in developing bio-
ethanol technology and that technology would become available for commercial  
exploitation by the end of this year.  The Committee congratulates  the Department 
on its success and hopes that the Depart ment would be in a position to make 
available the technology for commercial us e by the year end.  The Committee 
further recommends that the Department sh ould earnestly explore and expedite its 
Research & Development in the field of bi o-energy & bio-fuels for developing a cost 
effective, viable commercial alternative fo r conventional fuel at the earliest. The 
Committee also recommends that Government should provide adequate funds to the 
Department so that resource crunch does not come in the way of the Department in 
meeting this goal.

manuals, e-lab contents etc. have also been developed by teachers and students under this 
scheme. 
10.4 As regards the development of skilled manpower for Biotech industries in the 
country, the Department stated  that it had been implem enting the Biotech Industry 
Training Programme (BITP) since 11
th Plan, for providing practical industrial training for 
six months to fresh B.E./B.Tech./M.Sc./M.Te ch. students in biotechnology to improve 
their employment prospects.  About 3000 candidates had been  provided training in 
biotech industries and 30% of them had b een absorbed in industry. Considering the 
success of the programme, it would be contin ued by increasing number of intake from 
year to year during 12th Plan.   
10.5 The Committee is of the opinion that the development of skilled and quality 
human resource to cater to the rising needs of the biotech industry, which has 
grown many folds over the last few years, is a major challenge for the country. The 
Committee commends the human resou rce development initiatives of the 
Department, such as the initiation of the three year M.Sc./MBA dual degree 
programme in Biotechnology and Bio-en terprise Management, the Biotech 
Education and Skill Development Council and its ‘Star College Scheme’etc.  The 
Committee is further happy to note that th e Star College Scheme of the Department 
has led to increase in the number of students opting for life science courses, 
increased passed percentage and enhanced en rolment of students for higher studies 
in science courses and all candidates traine d by it in Biotech Industries have been 
absorbed  in the industry.  The Committee recommends that the Department should 
be provided adequate funds by the Government for its Human Resources 
Development Programme.  
11. PUBLICATIONS OF THE DEPARTMENT 
11.1 The Committee notes with happiness th at gross budgetary support for the science 
and technology sector had significantly increased during the last decade and the impact of 
such increase was becoming evident from the fact that India ranks 9
th globally in the 
number of scientific publications and 12th in the number of patents filed.  The Composite 
Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of In dian publications is around 12+ 1% and India’s global 
share has increased from 1.8% in 2001 to 3.5%  in 2011. But the percentage of Indian 
publications in the top 1% impact maki ng journals is only 2.5%.  The Science, 
Technology and Innovation Policy, 2013, also envisages that by 2020, the global share of 
publications must double and the number of papers in the top 1% journals must quadruple 
from the current levels.  The citation impact  of Indian publications must improve and 
match at least the world average.  Initiatives under the new policy should enable these 
macro indicators of research to be achieved by 2020. 
11.2 The Department, during the delibe rations of the Committee held on 3
rd April, 
2013, informed in reply to a query, that  during the year 2012-13, a total of 1467 
publications were brought out by the Departme nt. Out of these 363 publications had an 
impact factor above 5, while 1104 publica tions had an impact factor below 5. The 
Committee was also informed that in case the impact factor is more than five, then the 
publication is considered as a major journal publications. 

11.3 The Committee notes the number of research publications of the Department 
and hopes that in consonance with the Sc ience, Technology and Innovation Policy, 
2013, the Department would gear its efforts towards doubling the global share of its 
publications and quadrupling the existing number of its papers in the top 1% 
journals by 2020.   
12. BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT 
12.1 The main objectives of the program me were to promote the use of 
biotechnological processes and tools for the benefit of entrepreneurs and to create 
platform for employment generation among the target population and diffusion of proven 
and field-tested technologies  through demonstration, trai ning and extension activities. 
The main areas of focus were biof ertilizer production, vermicomposting, honey 
production, poultry, fish producti on, artificial insemination, mushroom cultivation, goat 
rearing, silk worm rearing, fruit plant nurse ries, ambulatory clinic s, sericulture and 
women health care. Till now, about 45,000 rura l, SC/ST and women population had been 
benefited through implementation of these programmes. Some of the successful examples 
of innovative societal programme include th e running of mobile am bulatory clinics for 
the farmers, low cost poly house construction for rais ing nursery-planting material for 
cultivation of medicinal and aromatic plants etc.  
12.2 As regards the Budgetary allocati on for the ‘Biotechnology for Societal 
Development’, the Committee observed that  an amount of Rs. 13.00 crores and Rs.10.15 
crores was allocated at B.E. & R.E. stages in the year 2012-13 and the allocation had 
been raised to Rs.12.00 crores in B.E. 2013-14 as compared to R.E. 2012-13. Explaining 
the reasons for the increase, the Department stated that the projects under the scheme 
were supported based on competitive grant system and the allocations fluctuate from year 
to year based on trends of expenditure and the number of applica tions received. These 
interventions were mainly on proven and fi eld tested technologies related to agro-
technologies, animal husbandry, etc. The De partment is implementing these projects 
through-out the country for socio-economic upl iftment of the SC/ST, Rural and Women 
population including backward community th rough competitive research grant scheme 
and the support was provided to various Govt . Institutes/ Universities, Krishi Vigyan 
Kendra (KVKs) and also to the Non-Govt. Organizations in various states of the country 
including North-eastern st ates and J&K region. Programmes supported for socio-
economic upliftment of the SC/ST, Rural and Women population including backward 
ones had received appreciation from all quarter s. Besides, an expert committee had been 
formed, consisting of a special group of experts working at the interface between 
technology and society were carefully chosen which annually evaluates these 
programmes and suggests new programmes.   
12.3 The Committee appreciates the programme initiated by the Department to 
promote the use of biotechnological pr ocesses and tools for the benefit of 
entrepreneurs and to create a platform for employment generation among the 
target population and diffusion of proven and field-tested technologies through 
demonstration, training and extension acti vities.  The Committee also notes with 
appreciation that the successful  examples of the programme inter-alia includes the 
running of mobile ambulatory clinics for the farmers, low cost poly house 
construction for raising nursery-planting material for cultivation of medicinal and 
aromatic plants etc. The Committee, however, would like the Department to develop 
a mechanism to actually assess as to what extent the programme has actually helped 
‘benefitted persons’ to get gainfully employed or become entrepreneurs. 

13. INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
13.1 The Committee was informed that the br oad areas of collaboration would include 
human resource development,  agriculture & food, medical & healthcare, molecular 
biology, bioinformatics & computational biolog y besides industrial collaborations. The 
Department was presently implementing bila teral/multilateral collaborations with 
developed countries such as Australia, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Netherlands, 
Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, United State of America, Europe 
etc. and there are a total of 180 ongoing prog rammes. The advantages of the programme 
include scientific exchanges with advanced countries, more  than 400 joint research 
publications, 27 patents, development of 4 software & 6 technologi es and 5 technology 
transfers to Indian industries.  
13.2 ‘International Cooperation’ had been  allocated a budget of Rs. 39.40 crores at                
R.E. stage in 2012-13, which had been increased to Rs. 50.00 crores at B.E. 2013-14. The 
Department explained that the allocation ha s been increased to meet the commitments 
during the year 2013-2014, which include seve ral new initiatives su ch as the Indo-UK 
collaboration in Animal Biotechnology;  DBT - Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation 
(BMGF) Memorandum of Understanding on hea lth, food and nutritional security needs 
of India & developing countri es and new phase of Indo-Sw iss collaboration in food 
security and climate change related to Indian agriculture.  
13.3 In reply to a clarification sought by the Committee, the Department stated that in 
the field of International Cooperation, the Indo-Swiss programme is an ongoing 
programme since 1998 under the agreement betw een Indian and Swiss Governments for 
implementing joint projects in agriculture a nd environment relevant to Indian conditions. 
The programme was implemented in phases of three years each in a network mode along 
the value chain from basic research to product development a nd technology transfer. 
Products have been developed and transferre d to industry, in three phases from 1998, 
through continued support viz. in sect resistant chickpea; bio-fertilizer for rice and wheat; 
bio-pesticide for legume pests and biosenso r for pesticide residue  detection. These 
products are being pursued fo r regulatory clearances and commercialization through PPP 
mode, it was decided jointly to launch new programme a nd therefore the Indo-Swiss 
programme was relaunched. The call for proposals had been advertised and the new 
phase will be launched based on peer review and relevance to the objectives during 2013-
2014.    
13.4 The Committee is pleased to know that ma ny useful products such as insect 
resistant chickpea; bio-fertilizer for rice and wheat; bio-pesticide for legume pests 
and biosensor for pesticide residue detectio n, have been developed as a result of 
Indo-Swiss programme and these products are being pursued for regulatory 
clearances and commercialisation usin g PPP mode.  The Committee recommends 
that the Department should focus more on  international collaboration that would 
bring direct benefit to the country particular ly those that would lead to technology 
transfer to Indian industries.  
14. PROGRAMME FOR PROMOTION OF EXCELLENCE & INNOVATION 
14.1 The Programme for Promotion for Excelle nce & Innovation consists of two major 
heads viz. Centres of Excellence and set ting up of Translational Research Centres 
andPlatforms. The Committee was informed that  the Department proposes to continue its 
ongoing 15 Centres of Excellence, 49 Pr ogramme Support and 13 individual R&D 
Projects during the 12
th Plan, keeping in view the excel lent output from the programme. 
In the year 2013-14, five new Centres of Ex cellence for translational science and high-

level innovative research in the areas su ch as system biology, synthetic biology, 
genomics, RNA biology, proteomics, metabolomic s, clinical neurosciences etc. were 
proposed to be established. Besides, the Department proposes to setup over 5 Technology 
Transfer Organizations (TTO ) spread across the country with ten professionals per 
institution to support IPR cells and resource pe rsons in various universities and 
institutions. 
14.2 The Committee observed that the allo cation for ‘Programme for promotion of 
Excellence & Innovation’ was decreased margin ally from Rs. 55.00 crores at B.E. stage 
to Rs. 53.00 crores at R.E. stage in the year 2012-13, however, in B.E. 2013-14 allocation 
has been increased substantially to Rs. 65.00 crores. Informing the Committee of the 
reasons for the increase in B.E. 2013-14 a llocation, the Department  stated that the 
programme for promotion of excellence & inno vations includes new initiatives such as 
establishment of atleast 20 inter-institutional centres and partnerships centres proposed 
during the 12
th Plan. While one such programme in pa rtnership with Indi an Institute of 
Science in modern biology had been sanctioned in 2012-2013, three more programmes in 
chemical biology, drug design etc. had been developed and were being implemented in 
2013-2014 and accordingly, increased provision  had been made during 2013-2014 for 
these commitments.   
14.3 The Committee takes note of the proposal of the Department to set up  five 
new Centres of Excellence fo r translational science and high-level innovative 
research in the cutting edge areas of biotechnology as also the proposal to setup over 
five Technology Transfer Organizations  (TTO) spread across the country for 
supporting IPR cells. The Committee is awa re of the urgent need for augmenting 
and strengthening of the basic and transl ational research capacity in areas of 
biotechnology and therefore the initiatives taken by the Department in this direction 
are welcome.  The Committee, however, woul d like to caution th e Department that 
its Centre of Excellence  should be manne d by deserving & capable professionals, 
appointed solely on merit, so that high level innovative research could be carried out 
in these centres and purpose of establishing these centres could be achieved.  
15. SMALL BUSINESS INNOVATION RE SEARCH INITIATIVE (SBIRI) 
AND BIOTECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY PARTNERSHIP PROGRAMME (BIPP)-
PUBLIC PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP 
15.1 The Public Private Partnership Programm e of the Department consists of two 
components viz. Small Business Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI) and 
Biotechnology Industry Partnership Programme (BIPP) schemes. SBIRI is the pioneering 
programme of the department that supports  R&D, process and product development in 
the biotech industry. The Department had so  far received more than 900 proposals and 
had sanctioned 105 projects under the sche me. Around 540 industr ies throughout the 
country had approached the De partment seeking support under  the scheme and presently 
82 projects were in operation. Under thes e programmes, 20 technologies had been 
developed and 6 of them had been comm ercialized. Similarly, the Biotechnology 
Industry Partnership Programme(BIPP) for high risk innovation research had been funded 
in partnership with the industry since 2010-2011. So far 102 projects have been approved 
and agreements signed with 85 companies with a commitment of Rs.777.00 crores, out of 
which the Department’s contribution under BIPP was Rs. 288.00 crores only, whereas the 
contribution of the private sector companies was Rs. 489.00 crores. Therefore, the private 
sector contribution is nearly 60% as compared to 40% by the Government.  

15.2 The Committee also noted that the alloca tion for ‘Public Privat e Partnership’ had 
shown a decreasing trend. The B.E. allocation of Rs. 139.00 cr ores was reduced to Rs. 
106.75 crores at R.E. stage in the year 2012-13 and at the B.E. stage of 2013-14 it has 
been further reduced to Rs.90.00 crores. Explaining the reasons for the decreasing trend, 
the Department stated that the decrease in allocation was due to th e decreasing trend of 
expenditure and availability of techno-eco nomically viable projects. Further, the 
Department stated that the biotech industry was at a nascent stage at the beginning of 11
th 
Plan and the size of the industry was relativ ely small with about 300 Small and Medium 
Enterprises (SMEs) and 25 major Indian comp anies who were eligible for funding. In 
order to increase the number of industries a nd accelerate the private sector R&D, several 
steps have been taken by the department viz. (i) road shows (ii) launching of ignition 
funds scheme from 2012-2013 for new star t-up companies (iii) establishment of 
incubators for providing common facilitie s to the start-up companies and (iv) 
establishment of Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC).  
15.3 The Committee commends the Departme nt on very encouraging results 
achieved from its SBIRI and BIPP progra mmes.  The Committee is pleased to note 
that SBIRI programmes have led to develo pment of 20 technologies out of which 6 
had already been commercialised. The success and popularity of BIPP programme 
in evident from the fact that 60% of  costs of projects undertaken under the 
programme have been funded by private sector.  The Committe e recommends that 
Department should take large number of projects under these programme so that a 
large base of biotech industries is estab lished in the country and greater private 
sectors investment flows in R&D in Biotechnology, apart from substantially 
increasing India’s share in global trade in biotechnology.  
16. PROJECTS/SCHEMES FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE NORTH–EASTERN 
AREAS & SIKKIM 
16.1 The Department informed that it had been  mandatorily allocating 10% of its total  
Budgetary outlay since the year 2007-2008, for the projects/schemes specifically 
designed for the benefit of the North-East ern region and Sikkim, for Human Resource 
Development, Biotechnology infrastructure and Research & Development in priority 
areas of North East in collaboration and part nership with other public  sector institutions 
& universities and even the private sector. 
16.2 The Committee noted that in the year 2012-13, the Department was allocated a 
Plan allocation of Rs. 148.50 crores in B.E., which was later reduced to Rs. 130.00 crores 
at the  R.E. stage. For the current fiscal 2013-14, the same amount i.e. Rs. 148.5 crores at 
B.E. stage had again been allocated and hence there was no change in the allocation to 
North East areas & Sikkim in 2013-2014 as compared to 2012-2013. In reply to a query 
regarding the adequacy of the funds allo cated, the Department explained that the 
allocations for the projects/schemes of the North Eastern region and Sikkim in HRD, 
bioinformatics, R&D and other schemes are made on the basis of actual assessment of the 
absorption capacity of these schemes. Th e North Eastern Region-Biotechnology 
Programme Management Cell (NER-BPMC) wh ich was established by the Department, 
in the year 2009 for evolving and implemen ting various programmes in the area of 
biotechnology for the benefit of North Ea stern Region, also suggests budgetary 
requirements based on continuous assessment. The Department added that as per the 
demands made by the NER-BPMC, the funds allocated were suffi cient to meet the 
requirements of the various projects/schemes specifically for the benefit of the North-
Eastern region and Sikkim.  

16.3 The Committee also noted that as per the Budget Circular 2013-14, issued by the 
Ministry of Finance(Departme nt of Economic Affairs), ou t of the three constituent 
Departments of the Ministry of Scien ce & Technology, only the Department of 
Biotechnology had been given the responsibil ity of spending 10% of its Annual Budget 
in the North Eastern Region, while the Departme nts of Scientific & Industrial Research 
and Science & Technology had been specifically exempted from spending the said 
amount, by the Ministry of Development of the North Eastern Region. 
16.4 The Committee notes that the Department has been mandatorily allocating 
10% of its total Budgetary outlay since the year 2007-2008, for the projects/schemes 
specifically designed for the benefit of the North-Eastern region and Sikkim, for 
Human Resource Development, Biotechnology infrastructure and Research & 
Development in priority areas of North Ea st in collaboration and partnership with 
other public sector institutions & univers ities and even the private sector.  The 
Committee recommends that the Department should carry out a study to assess to 
what extent its programmes in North-Eastern states  and Sikkim have been able to 
achieve their objectives and goals so that based on the results of this study, if 
needed, programmes could be further d ovetailed to the specific needs and 
requirements of the region and made more useful and effective.    
16.5 The Committee also pointed out in its 228
th Report that keeping in view the good 
performance of the programme in North-Ea st and Sikkim, the Department should not 
only continue its mandatory al location of 10% for this sect or but also to the extent 
possible, the budgetary allocation should be leveraged to  bring in more funds for the 
North-Eastern     states through PPP mode . The Committee further recommended in the 
said report that the Department should e xplore the possibility of earmarking some 
percentage of mandatory allocation to othe r backward regions including the Himalayan 
sector.  
16.6      In 238th Action Take n Report, the Department rep lied in response to aforesaid 
recommendation of the Committee that seve ral steps had been taken to implement 
industry oriented development programmes to promote Public Privat e Partnership in the 
North East. For this purpose, the active i nvolvement of ICAR, CSIR and DST and S&T 
Council had taken place for implementation of the industry-orie nted programme. In 
response to the Committee’s recommendation for earmarking certain percentage of 
mandatory allocation to other backward regions including Himalayan sector, the 
Department mentioned that a Committee had been constituted to work out the strategy for 
earmarking a certain percentage of funds for implementation during 2013-14.  
16.7 The Department further added that th e issue was being examined by subject 
specific Task Force Committees, instead of a single Committee due to the multi-
disciplinary aspect of the biotechnology. Based on the experience of implementing such 
provision and programmes in the North Easter n region on a mandatory basis, it had been 
observed by the Department that to en sure capacity building in Human Resource 
Development and Research & Developmen t, the projects received from the 
biotechnology-deficient universi ties/institutions across the country should be treated as 
“capacity building projects” and reviewed & funded separately from that of high capacity 
universities/institutions so as to ensure in clusiveness in terms of  overall development of 
life science and biotechnology capacity in  the country. Accordingly, in 2012-2013 
several projects have been funded in universities in biotechnology deficient states such as 
Bihar, Chattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh fo r overall developmen t of life sciences 

department in these universities. In 2013-2014, the strategy would be implemented across 
all the schemes under the Department.   
16.8 In the meeting of the Committee held on the 3rd April, 2013, the Department also 
pointed out that the le sson of rapid capacity building in a scientifically backward region, 
learnt through its experience in the North Ea stern region can be utilised in the other 
backward regions as well. The Department al so suggested that inst ead of allocating a 
fixed percentage of the total outlay for the North- Eastern region every year; the 
programme can be made more goal oriente d. In the goal dependent orientation, the 
emphasis would be on achievi ng the targeted goals with in a fixed period and the 
budgetary allocation may vary accordingly every year depending on the requirement.  
16.9 The Committee appreciates the action  taken by the Department on its 
aforesaid recommendation.  The Committee is happy that the Department is making 
sincere efforts to implemen t industry oriented developm ent programmes in Public 
Private Partnership mode in North East a nd hopes this would help in growth of 
Biotech industries in North East and help in development of this region.  The  
Committee is also happy to note that in 2012-2013 several projects have been funded 
in universities in biotechnology deficient states such as Bihar, Chattisgarh and 
Madhya Pradesh for overall development of  life sciences de partment in these 
universities.  The Committee  recommends th at it should also implement industry 
oriented development in Public Privat e Partnership mode in other backward 
regions of the country including Himalaya n region to help growth of Biotech 
industries in these regions as well. The Committee further recommends that in 
order to assess the potency and utility of its training programmes, the Department 
should develop a mechanis m to find out as to what extent these training 
programmes have actually resulted in trained persons becoming gainfully employed 
or becoming entrepreneurs because that alone will demonstrate the usefulness of 
these programmes. 
17. BIO-SECURITY AND BIO-TERRORISM 
17.1 During the deliberations of the Committee, held on the 3
rd April, 2013, the issues 
relating to the Bio-security and Bio-terrorism were also discussed. The Department stated 
that earlier there was no database on the work done in the country on biotechnology 
relating to release of dangerous bio-organism s from laboratories, but the same is being 
created now. The Department further inform ed that in this connection, Bio-safety 
Laboratories (BSL) had been created which we re highly secured. It  was also informed 
that a Memorandum of Understanding had been signed with the Defence Research and 
Development Organisation. The Department al so emphasised the need  for international 
collaboration in this field.  
17.2 The Committee is happy to note that th e Department has become sufficiently 
sensitized of the risk of bio-terrorism  and has initiated steps to deal with it. The 
Committee is also pleased to know of th e setting up of Bio-safety Laboratories, 
which are highly secured. The Committee ho pes that further necessary measures in 
this respect would be taken by the Government at the earliest.    
18. The Committee after examining the var ious aspects of the Demands for 
Grants (2013-14) of the De partment of Bio-Technology, is of the view that the 
Department, through its various schemes and programmes, apart from promoting 
research & development in biotechnology, has demonstrated the ability to use this 
technology for societal benefit. Some of th e initiatives of the Departments discussed 
above are commendable and if properly implemented will bring immense benefits to 

the targeted groups.  The Committee, while ta king note of it, is of the opinion that 
programmes of the Department deserve to be adequately funded by the 
Government.
